cloudwatch.name: CloudWatch metrics & alarms
cloudwatch.role: Measure workload behaviour; alarm on a defined statistic, dimension and time window.
bullets: EC2 basic monitoring usually publishes at five-minute intervals; detailed monitoring usually changes this to one minute. Memory and filesystem utilisation need an agent or custom publisher.

Standard-resolution custom metrics use one-minute resolution; high-resolution metrics can publish at one second. Pick a supported alarm period and statistic; percentile latency and average latency answer different questions. Select the metric’s storage resolution when publishing with PutMetricData.

M out of N means at least M breaching datapoints among N evaluated periods. Missing, breaching, notBreaching and ignore have different outcomes. Composite alarms combine alarm states; they do not support Auto Scaling actions directly.

Use metric math for an error rate; publish both failed and total requests. Dashboards visualise data, alarms evaluate it. Cross-account observability links source accounts to a monitoring account within a Region; cross-Region dashboards are a separate capability.
cloudwatch.boundary: Choose an alarm for a recurring condition; use Logs Insights to investigate individual events. Neither creates a missing memory metric.
cloudwatch.investigate: Check namespace, dimensions, statistic, units, period, timestamps, ingestion delay and TreatMissingData before changing the threshold. Confirm the SNS subscription and alarm actions are enabled.
cloudwatch.remediate: Correct the metric or action configuration; publish a controlled test value and verify state history plus delivery. Avoid testing destructive actions against production.
cloudwatch.example:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name high-cpu \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --statistic Average --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 \
  --datapoints-to-alarm 2 --threshold 80 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data missing
cloudwatch.trigger: Need an automatic response to sustained metric behaviour → alarm, then an appropriate action.
cloudwatch.trap: Detailed monitoring changes frequency, not the list of guest OS metrics. Composite alarms can notify or trigger supported operations; use underlying metric alarms for scaling.
cloudwatch.analogy: The dashboard is the instrument panel; the alarm is the rule that decides when to ring.

notes.title: Canary test, custom schedule, or trace correlation?
notes.flow:
Scheduled canary → managed Lambda-based test → endpoint → metrics + artifacts → alarm
Existing request telemetry → correlated trace/map → investigation
paragraphs: CloudWatch Synthetics canaries run scheduled endpoint/browser scripts. Lambda functions perform the work underneath; Synthetics supplies monitoring integrations, metrics and test artifacts.

Scheduled Lambda can implement a custom check, but you assemble its schedule, measurements, reporting, artifact retention and alarms. Prefer the purpose-built monitor when those managed capabilities are the deciding requirement.

ServiceLens is older exam terminology for correlating metrics, logs and traces; it does not execute browser tests. Current docs combine ServiceLens/service maps into the X-Ray trace map and describe Application Signals for application observability.
notes.trigger: Scheduled customer-journey validation, even with no real traffic → Synthetics; investigate an existing slow request → traces/logs/correlation.
notes.trap: Dashboards display evidence; metric alarms evaluate metrics; composite alarms combine alarm states. None is the endpoint test executor.

cloudwatch.flow: Resource / agent → metric → alarm evaluation → configured action → verified outcome.

logs.name: Logs, queries & traces
logs.role: Find the event or downstream operation behind an aggregate symptom.
bullets: CloudWatch Agent collects guest logs and metrics; its IAM role, configuration, network access and log retention must be managed. Container Insights supports ECS/EKS operational telemetry.
A metric filter turns matching incoming log events into metric values for future alarms. Logs Insights queries retained log data; it does not retroactively populate a metric filter.
X-Ray/OpenTelemetry traces correlate request segments and downstream subsegments. Sampling limits volume; an absent trace is not proof that no request occurred.

Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus stores and queries Prometheus metrics; Amazon Managed Grafana presents dashboards. Monitor Lambda errors, duration, throttles and concurrency, plus Bedrock latency, invocation errors and quotas for AI workloads.
logs.boundary: Use logs for event detail, traces for where one request spent time and metrics for trends. Set retention and query windows to control cost.
logs.investigate: Correlate timestamps, request IDs, deployment version and trace ID. Confirm agent status, log stream timestamps, IAM permissions and ingestion before interpreting an empty query.
logs.remediate: Repair collection or instrumentation; reproduce one known request and confirm its log and downstream trace. Redact secrets and personal data at source.
logs.example:
# CloudWatch Logs Insights query (query editor)
fields @timestamp, @message, requestId
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count(*) as errors by bin(5m)
logs.trigger: Alarm says latency rose; need the slow dependency → correlated trace and application logs.
logs.trap: A trace is not an API audit log. Detailed EC2 monitoring does not install a log collector.
logs.analogy: Metrics count late deliveries; logs record each delivery; a trace follows one parcel through the depots.
logs.flow: Application / guest → configured collector → logs / traces → correlated query → hypothesis.

trail.name: CloudTrail & change evidence
trail.role: Record supported AWS API activity: who acted, what changed and from where.
bullets: Event history provides recent management events in each Region. Trails deliver ongoing events; configure multi-Region and organisation coverage deliberately.
Data events, such as supported S3 object operations, require appropriate event selectors and have separate cost. A management trail is not automatically an object access log.

Log file validation supports integrity checking. Protect log buckets with least privilege, encryption, retention and deletion controls. Query long-term logs with Athena or supported CloudTrail analysis tools.
trail.boundary: Choose CloudTrail for API identity and change time; Config explains resource configuration history; ALB logs explain HTTP requests.
trail.investigate: Search around the incident for eventName, userIdentity, errorCode, requestParameters and sourceIPAddress in the correct account/Region.
trail.remediate: Correct the unauthorised or accidental change through controlled tooling; verify the resource state and a new successful operation, then prevent recurrence with policy or automation.
trail.trigger: Who removed the ingress rule? → CloudTrail management event.
trail.trap: CloudTrail does not replace application logs, packet capture or a Config compliance rule.
trail.analogy: A signed change register, rather than a live health monitor.
trail.flow: Supported AWS API activity → event record → identity/change investigation.

events.name: EventBridge, SNS & remediation
events.role: Turn a matching operational event into a notification or a controlled recovery action.
bullets: EventBridge rules match event patterns on a bus; Scheduler handles time-based invocations. Input transformers change target input, not the source resource.
SNS fans notifications to subscribed endpoints; confirm subscriptions and delivery permissions. SQS buffers work with visibility timeouts, retries and dead-letter queues.
Use Lambda for bounded custom logic, Systems Manager Automation for a runbook and Step Functions for state, waits, retries and approvals. Standard and Express workflow semantics differ.
Check EventBridge target retry policy and DLQ. A DLQ is an investigation queue, not automatic successful recovery. Make actions idempotent and constrain their role.
events.boundary: An event routes work; a runbook owns the operational procedure. Use a schedule when the requirement is a recurring time, not a resource-state transition.
events.investigate: Check the event bus, exact JSON pattern, MatchedEvents/FailedInvocations, target role or resource policy, DLQ and downstream execution history.
events.remediate: Test the pattern, fix target access and safely replay/reprocess eligible failures; verify the resource outcome as well as target invocation.
events.trigger: React to a resource event → EventBridge; notify people → SNS; execute a repeatable multi-step repair → Automation.
events.trap: A matched rule does not prove the target ran or that the repair worked. Avoid recursive remediation loops.
events.analogy: The switchboard dispatches a ticket; the runbook is the repair procedure.

notes.title: Notify on creation, not every transition or datapoint
notes.flow:
EC2 RunInstances → CloudTrail API event → EventBridge rule → SNS
Direct EC2 state event → EventBridge is a separate event path
paragraphs: To distinguish new launches from restarting existing instances, match the RunInstances API event in the appropriate CloudTrail/EventBridge setup. EC2 pending/running events also occur on starts of existing instances.
EventBridge also receives direct service events without CloudTrail. Choose the event that identifies the required operation rather than adding an audit dependency to every event flow.

Logs → metric filter → alarm can be appropriate for aggregated conditions, but is a more complex route for individual event notifications. Alarm notifications normally follow state transitions; repeated matching events while already ALARM are not one notification each.
notes.trigger: Notify about each matching new launch API operation → event pattern and target, not a metric alarm that stays ALARM.
notes.trap: One RunInstances call can launch multiple instances; one matching API event is not necessarily one notification per created instance. Transform/process IDs if the requirement is per instance.

events.flow: Operational event → matching rule → authorised target → bounded procedure → result.

ec2.name: EC2 performance & capacity
ec2.role: Operate instances with sufficient CPU, memory, storage and network capacity.
bullets: Distinguish instance status checks from system status checks; inspect OS logs and CloudWatch Agent metrics for guest failures.
T-family CPU credits can constrain sustained burst workloads. Network and EBS limits belong to the instance as well as the volume; changing only one can leave the bottleneck.
Use Compute Optimizer recommendations with representative workload metrics, tags and cost data. On-Demand, Spot and commitment discounts have different interruption and flexibility trade-offs.
Placement groups address specific latency, partition or failure-isolation needs. Capacity Reservations reserve capacity; a Savings Plan discounts eligible usage without reserving capacity.
ec2.boundary: Scale horizontally when the application supports more workers; resize when a single process needs more memory/CPU. Verify licensing, restart and architecture constraints.
ec2.investigate: Compare CPU, credit balance, memory, swap, NetworkIn/Out, EBS queue/latency and service latency over the same interval. A busy CPU is a signal, not a root cause.
ec2.remediate: Right-size, tune or replace through the launch template and instance refresh; measure throughput and latency after warm-up and maintain a rollback version.
ec2.trigger: Sustained CPU plus falling credit balance on burstable instances → investigate credits and instance family.
ec2.trap: Minimum ASG capacity is not a capacity reservation. A lower hourly price can cost more if it cannot meet the workload.
ec2.analogy: Check whether the machine is short of engine power, working space or road capacity before buying a larger engine.

notes.title: Resize: stop → change → start
notes.flow: Compatible EBS-backed instance → stop → change instance type → start → verify
paragraphs: In-place resizing requires compatibility and downtime. Stopping an ASG member can cause replacement unless maintenance is coordinated with ASG behaviour.

Instance ID, private IPv4, EIP and assigned IPv6 persist across ordinary stop/start; an auto-assigned public IPv4 normally changes. Instance-store contents are lost. EBS data persists according to its lifecycle.

Resizing changes the compatible EBS-root instance’s CPU/RAM configuration, not its AMI metadata or disk size. No manual root-volume move is required. An instance-store-root workload needs migration instead of this in-place path.

An EBS-root instance can also have instance-store disks. Their data survives a normal reboot, but is lost on stop/start, termination or underlying disk failure. Copy required data to persistent storage before maintenance.
notes.trigger: Need a larger compatible instance → account for stop/start downtime and the address clients use.
notes.trap: An Elastic IP and an auto-assigned public IPv4 do not have the same stop/start behaviour.

notes.title: Enhanced networking: capability versus implementation
notes.flow: Measure PPS / bandwidth / allowance counters → inspect instance + driver → select compatible networking
paragraphs: Enhanced networking uses SR-IOV; ENA is the modern implementation for Nitro-based instances. Some older families use Intel 82599 VF. Actual bandwidth/PPS constraints depend on instance type, size and traffic pattern.
An older practice explanation’s roughly 20K-PPS legacy-VIF clue is not a universal modern EC2 ceiling. Do not memorise old 10/25-Gbps figures as the limit of every current instance.

EFA targets tightly coupled HPC/AI communication. Direct Connect connects an on-premises network to AWS; neither is the general remedy for a legacy application instance’s network interface bottleneck.
notes.trigger: Legacy interface bottleneck on a compatible workload → examine enhanced networking/ENA and the exact instance limits.
notes.trap: Buying bandwidth does not necessarily fix a packet-rate or single-flow limit.

notes.title: API termination, OS shutdown and ASG are separate
notes.flow:
Direct TerminateInstances → DisableApiTermination check
OS shutdown → stop OR terminate setting
ASG scale-in / unhealthy replacement → separate ASG controls
paragraphs: DisableApiTermination=true blocks direct EC2 console/CLI/API termination. It does not block OS-initiated termination when InstanceInitiatedShutdownBehavior=terminate, or ASG scale-in/unhealthy replacement.

With shutdown behaviour stop, OS shutdown stops the EBS-root instance; a normally operating ASG may later replace that unhealthy member. Scale-in protection is another setting and does not block unhealthy replacement.
notes.trigger: First identify the actor and action: direct terminate, OS shutdown, scale-in or health replacement.
notes.trap: A question claiming immediate termination after shutdown assumes the terminate setting. Do not infer it from API termination protection alone.

notes.title: Capacity assurance versus commitment discounts
notes.flow:
Need launch capacity in AZ A → matching reservation
Need lower eligible usage price → RI / Savings Plan
Both requirements → compatible capacity and discount controls
paragraphs: A Capacity Reservation reserves matching AZ capacity, not a discount by itself. Immediate-start reservations have no fixed term; future-dated variants have commitment/cancellation conditions. Unused reserved capacity costs money; occupied capacity is not charged twice.

Eligible Regional RI/Savings Plan discounts can apply to matching Capacity Reservations. Sharing a reservation does not transfer ownership. Cluster placement groups are supported; older “no placement groups” explanations are outdated.

Savings Plans are spending commitments, not budget caps: unused commitment remains payable, while uncovered excess usage is On-Demand. Eligible Regional RIs offer size flexibility under documented platform/tenancy conditions.
notes.trigger: Guaranteed matching AZ capacity → capacity reservation / Zonal RI; cost-only commitment → discount mechanism.
notes.trap: ASG desired capacity, a Regional RI and a Savings Plan do not independently reserve AZ capacity.

rows: Immediate-start: no fixed term; future-dated variants differ
1/3 years; matching Region/configuration, eligible size flexibility
$/hour, 1/3 years; eligible EC2/Lambda/Fargate, broader family/Region flexibility

ec2.flow: Healthy launch configuration → instance → workload → resource measurements → controlled replacement/tuning.

ebs.name: EBS performance & snapshots
ebs.role: Provide persistent block storage within an Availability Zone; tune IOPS and throughput to the workload.
bullets: gp2 performance is tied to size and credits; gp3 separates provisioned performance from capacity. io2 is for demanding I/O requirements. HDD types suit supported sequential workloads, not boot volumes.
An EBS volume attaches to compatible instances in its own AZ. Multi-Attach is a specialised supported io1/io2 option, not a general cross-AZ shared filesystem.
Snapshots are incremental backups managed regionally and can create volumes in another AZ. Copy snapshots to another Region when recovery requires it; check KMS access.
New volumes restored from snapshots may need initialisation; Fast Snapshot Restore or supported provisioned volume initialisation options change readiness/cost.
ebs.boundary: Block disk → EBS. Shared files → EFS/FSx. Objects → S3. Check instance bandwidth before buying more volume IOPS.
ebs.investigate: Correlate VolumeQueueLength, read/write latency, throughput, IOPS, BurstBalance where applicable, free space and the instance EBS limits.
ebs.remediate: Modify the supported volume type/performance, extend the partition/filesystem separately when growing size, then validate latency and restore a sample snapshot.
ebs.example:
# Example only: check instance/volume requirements before applying
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --volume-type gp3 --iops 6000 --throughput 250
ebs.trigger: gp2 credits exhausted but disk size is already sufficient → consider gp3 performance settings.
ebs.trap: Increasing a volume size does not automatically expand every filesystem. A completed snapshot is not a tested application restore.
ebs.analogy: A disk has separate capacity, operations-per-second and delivery-bandwidth limits.

rows: IOPS tied to size; eligible burst credits
Check supported instance/volume capabilities and cost.

notes.title: Fast Snapshot Restore versus provisioned IOPS
notes.flow:
Snapshot (Regional) → enable FSR for destination AZ → wait Ready + credits
→ create new volume in that AZ → initialized blocks at creation
paragraphs: A snapshot is Regional; a working volume is AZ-specific. FSR is enabled per snapshot/AZ pair before creation and needs a ready state plus sufficient volume-creation credits. A copied or later snapshot does not automatically inherit FSR.

Within supported FSR performance capabilities, the new volume is fully initialised at creation, removing first-read lazy-loading latency. Higher provisioned IOPS does not by itself load snapshot blocks.

Modern EBS also offers a provisioned volume-initialisation rate for supported restores. That controls initialisation speed; it is not a promise that the new volume is fully ready instantly. Check current support, quotas and cost.

Enable FSR for the destination AZ, regardless of the original volume’s AZ. Charges run per snapshot per enabled AZ, per minute with a one-hour minimum, even without a restore; normal snapshot/volume charges remain separate. It improves first-I/O readiness, not simply API creation speed.
notes.trigger: First-read restore latency with immediate full initialisation required → prepare suitable FSR before volume creation.
notes.trap: “Preload in the AZ” is a mental model, not AWS’s documented internal storage implementation. Enabling FSR after creating the affected volume does not retroactively initialise it.

notes.title: Available volume, but attachment is stuck
notes.flow: Volume ID → AttachVolume device mapping → driver / OS device → mount
paragraphs: The volume ID, requested attachment name and guest-visible device name are different identifiers. Drivers, especially NVMe enumeration, can remap names; use volume IDs/stable filesystem identifiers to identify the intended disk.

If evidence points to a retained/busy device name after a detach, verify the guest’s devices and retry with an unused supported name. Also check same-AZ placement, attachment limits and actual attachment state before choosing a remedy.
notes.trigger: Driver/device-name collision → unused supported mapping, not more disk performance credits.
notes.trap: IOPS credits affect I/O performance, not whether the control plane can attach a disk. A stuck attachment alone does not prove which cause applies.
notes.example:
# Guest diagnostic example, Linux
lsblk -o NAME,SERIAL,SIZE,MOUNTPOINTS
# Compare with AWS volume ID/attachment mapping; do not format an unknown disk.

notes.title: Snapshot automation: lifecycle, central backup or five-minute API calls?
notes.flow:
rate(5 minutes) → EventBridge Scheduler execution role → EC2 CreateSnapshot
→ asynchronous snapshot completion → separate retention / deletion controls
paragraphs: DLM manages EBS snapshot creation/retention/deletion through the EC2 console or APIs. DLM custom schedules and AWS Backup scheduled snapshot rules have a one-hour minimum; supported continuous backup is a separate mechanism.
For every few minutes, use EventBridge Scheduler with a supported EC2 universal API target and execution role. Lambda is optional custom logic, not a mandatory hop or the schedule itself.

“CloudWatch Events” is historical terminology. Modern flexible schedules use EventBridge Scheduler. Scheduling creates recovery points but does not by itself implement retention, exact completion times or application-consistent capture. DLM cannot automatically adopt snapshots created by unrelated mechanisms.
notes.trigger: Explicit every-five-minutes snapshot API requirement → Scheduler; built-in hourly lifecycle → DLM.
notes.trap: Do not claim the EC2 console lacks automated snapshots, or that Lambda alone supplies recurrence.

rows: EBS snapshot creation, retention, deletion; hourly or less frequent
Snapshot creation every few minutes / flexible API scheduling

ebs.flow: EC2 block I/O ↔ same-AZ volume; snapshot → separately restored volume.

s3.name: S3 operations & protection
s3.role: Operate object storage with appropriate access, lifecycle, transfer and recovery controls.
bullets: Use multipart upload for suitable large objects; abort incomplete uploads with lifecycle rules. Transfer Acceleration can help long-distance uploads; benchmark before enabling it. DataSync automates supported bulk transfers.

Lifecycle transitions and expiration manage storage cost, subject to minimum durations, request/retrieval charges and retrieval latency. Versioning preserves older versions; a delete marker is not destruction of every version.

SRR/CRR replicate eligible new objects after configuration; use Batch Replication for existing objects. Replication needs versioning, permissions and encryption configuration. Lifecycle actions are not simply copied to the destination.
Keep access-log destination separate to avoid recursive logging. Block Public Access, bucket policies and Object Ownership govern access; an endpoint policy alone does not grant bucket access.
s3.boundary: Versioning recovers an overwritten object; replication maintains another copy; AWS Backup and Object Lock address different retention/recovery needs.
s3.investigate: For 403: inspect principal, bucket/access-point policy, explicit denies, KMS access and endpoint restrictions. For slow transfers: check request concurrency, object sizes and network path.
s3.remediate: Restore the required version or correct access/transfer settings; verify checksum, version ID, encryption and an application read. Test recovery from accidental deletion.
s3.example:
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket example-orders --prefix invoices/
# Retrieve an explicitly selected version (replace placeholders)
aws s3api get-object --bucket example-orders --key invoices/42.pdf \
  --version-id VERSION_ID recovered.pdf
s3.trigger: Recover overwritten data → version ID; copy existing objects under a replication policy → Batch Replication.
s3.trap: Replication can copy unwanted changes and is not an independent historical backup. Storage class changes can alter recovery time and cost.
s3.analogy: Version history is a filing cabinet; replication is a second cabinet that follows configured changes.

notes.title: Retain until is not delete at
notes.flow:
Versioning + Object Lock → retain protected version → retention expires
→ version becomes eligible → configured Lifecycle action eventually deletes eligible data
paragraphs: Object Lock protects object versions. Retain Until Date ending makes a version deletable under the applicable policies; it does not itself schedule deletion. Legal holds and remaining controls can still block it.

Use versioning and an appropriate retention mode for the stated requirement, then Lifecycle for eligible expiration/cleanup. Include noncurrent versions and delete markers in the design. Governance bypass and compliance retention have different rules.
“Keep for five years” describes a requirement; it does not prove the existing bucket already has Object Lock configured.
notes.trigger: Cannot delete before retention + automatic cleanup afterwards → retention control plus suitable lifecycle/version rules.
notes.trap: Lifecycle does not bypass an active lock, and a simple delete marker does not erase a retained version.

notes.title: API audit and server access logging are different evidence
notes.flow:
Management API → CloudTrail management event
GetObject / PutObject → explicitly selected CloudTrail data events
Bucket access request → best-effort server access log delivery
paragraphs: S3 object-level CloudTrail data events must be explicitly configured and are charged separately; a management trail does not automatically include them.

For server access logging delivered directly to an S3 bucket there is no additional log-delivery charge; storage, access and analysis still cost money. Delivery is best effort and should not be treated as a complete immediate audit feed. Keep the source and log destination separate.
Current AWS documentation also offers CloudWatch Logs delivery with vended-log ingestion pricing. Do not generalise the S3 delivery pricing statement to every log destination.
notes.trigger: Need object API caller evidence → configure data-event coverage; compare the required completeness and costs.
notes.trap: “No delivery fee” does not mean free storage or guaranteed complete real-time delivery.

notes.title: Physical import ends in S3, then Lifecycle
notes.flow:
Ship device → copy on premises → return device → AWS imports to S3
→ configured Lifecycle transition → eligible S3 Glacier storage class
paragraphs: Snowball Edge import moves locally copied data back to AWS before the S3 import completes. A Lifecycle rule then controls eligible storage-class transitions; the device does not directly deliver objects into a Glacier-class archive.

Availability caveat: since 7 November 2025, Snowball Edge is available only to existing customers. Treat older exam scenarios accordingly; new customers should evaluate current online/physical-transfer alternatives.
notes.trigger: An eligible existing customer needs offline bulk import, then archive storage → device import to S3 plus Lifecycle.
notes.trap: Shipping, import completion and a later storage-class transition are different stages.

s3.flow: Authorised object request → bucket/object version → response; lifecycle and recovery are separate operations.

files.name: EFS, FSx & S3 Files
files.role: Choose and operate shared storage by protocol, application semantics and recovery needs.
bullets: Regional EFS provides shared NFS access through mount targets in selected AZs; permit NFS and resolve the mount DNS name. EFS One Zone has a different resilience boundary.

FSx offerings serve specific filesystem workloads, such as Windows SMB, Lustre, ONTAP and OpenZFS. Match protocol, deployment model, throughput and snapshots/backup support. For supported Windows workloads, file version recovery can involve configured shadow copies; distinguish file-level versions from whole-filesystem backups.
S3 Files provides file access to S3 data through a managed filesystem; inspect its access, consistency and storage-class behaviour rather than treating an object bucket as an ordinary block disk.
Use lifecycle and throughput settings deliberately. Storage Gateway supports hybrid access patterns; DataSync moves supported data, rather than replacing the live application filesystem.
files.boundary: Shared Linux files across AZs → regional EFS; Windows-specific SMB/AD requirements → suitable FSx. Choose object APIs when file semantics are unnecessary.
files.investigate: Check mount target placement, DNS, NFS/SMB security rules, client identity, throughput mode, storage latency and application access pattern.
files.remediate: Correct mounts/access or throughput, test concurrent access from both AZs and perform a supported backup/restore test.
files.example:
# NFS example with amazon-efs-utils installed; mount target/network access required
sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-0123456789abcdef0:/ /mnt/shared
files.trigger: Multiple instances need the same persistent files across AZs → a regional shared filesystem.
files.trap: EBS is not a general cross-AZ shared filesystem. An S3 Glacier object may require restoration before S3 Files can read it.
files.analogy: EBS is a machine’s disk; a shared filesystem is a network filing room; S3 is an object repository.

rows: Mount targets, NFS access, throughput and lifecycle.
Specific SMB / Lustre / ONTAP / OpenZFS semantics
Supported access/consistency and object storage-class behaviour.
Same-AZ attachment; not general cross-AZ file sharing.

files.flow: Application file call → configured mount/identity → shared filesystem → result.

asg.name: Auto Scaling & elasticity
asg.role: Reconcile a group’s running capacity with desired capacity across configured AZs.
bullets: Min/max constrain desired capacity. Scaling policies change desired capacity; the ASG launches or terminates instances to reconcile actual capacity. Launches still depend on subnet IPs, quotas and available capacity.
Target tracking follows a proportional utilisation metric; step scaling uses alarm severity. Scheduled actions handle known times; predictive scaling uses supported forecast patterns.
Enable ELB health checks when the group must replace application-unhealthy targets. Use health-check grace periods and instance warm-up appropriately; they solve different timing problems.
Lifecycle hooks allow controlled launch/termination work. Instance refresh rolls out launch-template changes; configure healthy percentages, checkpoints and rollback.
asg.boundary: ASG manages instance count/health replacement; ALB distributes requests. A single ASG is regional and can span AZs, not Regions.
asg.investigate: Inspect scaling activities, suspended processes, desired versus InService capacity, launch-template version, subnet free IPs, health type and warm-up.
asg.remediate: Repair the failing launch/health dependency, then verify capacity reaches desired and the new targets pass application checks under load.
asg.example:
# Example: actual 3, desired 5; ChangeInCapacity +3 → desired 8 (if max permits)
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name orders-asg
asg.trigger: Predictable morning surge → scheduled scaling; changing utilisation → target tracking with a suitable metric.
asg.trap: Min=1 permits a single instance and does not ensure AZ redundancy. Low average CPU can hide a hot instance or a downstream bottleneck.
asg.analogy: The ASG is the staffing manager; the load balancer allocates incoming work.

notes.title: Scale-in protection: target count can differ from actual
notes.flow:
Policy lowers desired 4 → 3 → every member protected → actual remains 4
Remove selected protection → ASG can converge to desired
paragraphs: Desired capacity is a target. Scale-in protection can prevent the selected termination without preventing the target from decreasing. Inspect Activity history and actual member states.
Scale-in protection does not prevent unhealthy replacement. Group metrics must be enabled to publish the group series; use instance metrics for the individual machine.
notes.trigger: Desired fell but no instance was removed → inspect scale-in protection and scaling activity.
notes.trap: An in-service count is not a guarantee that every application is healthy; health/replacement is a separate process.

rows: Total, including in-service, pending and terminating

asg.flow: Metric / schedule → scaling policy → desired capacity → instance reconciliation → target health.

alb.name: Load balancing & target health
alb.role: Accept traffic on listeners and route it to registered targets using rules and health information.
bullets: ALB routes HTTP/HTTPS by host/path and other supported rules; NLB handles supported transport-layer requirements. Internet-facing frontends can reach private backend targets.
ALB cross-zone is on at load-balancer level; target-group settings can disable it. With cross-zone and equivalent targets, 2 in AZ A plus 8 in B means roughly 10% per target, not 50% per AZ.
Health checks use configured port, path, timeout, matcher and thresholds. A service can work directly yet fail its health check. If all targets are unhealthy, ALB can fail open.
Deregistration delay drains connections. Sticky sessions, routing algorithm and differing response times can create unequal request counts.
alb.boundary: Need HTTP routing → ALB. Need instance replacement → ASG with the relevant health checks. Need cross-Region entry/failover → DNS or Global Accelerator as appropriate.
alb.investigate: Inspect target-health reason, ALB versus target 5xx, TargetResponseTime and access logs. Check listener rule, target port, SG references and health endpoint dependencies.
alb.remediate: Correct the first failing boundary; verify repeated healthy checks, request success and latency. Do not make the health endpoint lie to hide a broken dependency.
alb.example:
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn TARGET_GROUP_ARN
# Illustration: browser → HTTPS:443 listener → /orders rule → HTTP:8080 target
alb.trigger: Requests fail only through the load balancer → compare health configuration, target rules and frontend/backend security.
alb.trap: Cross-zone distributes eligible traffic, not guaranteed equal request counts. An ALB is regional; it does not span Regions.
alb.analogy: The receptionist routes visitors; the building manager replaces a broken office.

notes.title: Health status is periodic; HTTP status is a request outcome
notes.flow:
Periodic probes → target health → eligible routing
Separate request → selected target → HTTP result
paragraphs: ALB does not run a fresh health check before every request. It uses periodically evaluated target health. With healthy targets available it normally avoids unhealthy ones; all registered targets unhealthy can cause fail-open routing.

Unhealthy does not automatically mean HTTP 503. No registered targets/all targets unused can produce an ALB 503; a backend application can independently return its own 503. Read target-health reasons and ALB versus target status evidence.

ASG uses enabled ELB health checks to replace the failed instance; it does not simply restart that application. One failed AZ is not necessarily every target failing: inspect healthy targets, cross-zone settings and whether there is one load balancer or several.
notes.trigger: Separate health state, routing eligibility, actual request status and ASG replacement.
notes.trap: A periodic health result can lag a new failure; all-unhealthy fail-open is not a guarantee of successful responses.

alb.flow: Client → listener → matching rule → target group → selected target → response.

rds.name: RDS, Aurora & database recovery
rds.role: Operate relational availability, read scaling, connections, performance and recovery.
bullets: A traditional Multi-AZ DB instance has a synchronous standby for failover, not read traffic. A Multi-AZ DB cluster has readable instances; Aurora has its own replicated storage and reader architecture.

Read replicas generally replicate asynchronously; route reads to their endpoints and monitor lag. Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts supported database capacity within configured limits; it does not remove query tuning.
Use CloudWatch Database Insights to analyse DB load, waits and SQL. Older study material calls out Performance Insights. RDS Proxy pools/manages connections; it does not repair inefficient SQL.

Automated backups support PITR within configured retention, up to 35 days for supported RDS DB instances. Manual snapshots persist until deleted. Restore creates a new database resource; plan endpoint cutover and KMS access.
rds.boundary: Host/AZ failure → Multi-AZ; read pressure with lag tolerance → read replicas; accidental logical change → PITR/snapshot restore.
rds.investigate: Compare CPU, FreeableMemory, storage latency/free space, connections, replica lag and DB-load waits. Check events and pending modifications/maintenance windows.
rds.remediate: Tune SQL/indexes or the limiting resource; test failover with reconnect logic. Restore to an isolated DB, validate records and redirect traffic only after checks.
rds.trigger: Deleted valid rows but database remains healthy → PITR, not a standby that replicated the deletion.
rds.trap: Failover is not historical recovery. A successful restore API response does not mean the new endpoint is ready or validated.
rds.analogy: A standby replaces a failed shop; a backup recovers the ledger from before a bad entry.

rows: One standby is not a reader.
Asynchronous lag; application selects read endpoint.
New resource; validate and plan cutover.
Does not fix inefficient SQL or transaction locks.

notes.title: MySQL replica: endpoint, writes & message limits
notes.flow:
Application writes → source endpoint → asynchronous replication → replica
Reporting reads → replica’s own endpoint
paragraphs: Each RDS instance has its own endpoint. MySQL read replicas normally reject application writes with read_only enabled. Setting read_only=0 permits writes, but conflicting changes can stop replication; a replica is not a second independently writable primary.
A replica-specific index is a documented special case requiring read_only=0 while it is created. Do not generalise that exception into permission for arbitrary application writes.

max_allowed_packet bounds an individual logical MySQL message, such as a statement, row or replication event. It is neither database capacity nor total transaction/write volume. A large message can break replication when the replica’s configured value is lower; matching source/replica parameter values removes that mismatch.
notes.trigger: Replication stopped with a packet-size error → compare parameter groups and the failing logical message.
notes.trap: A lower limit need not fail immediately: the problematic message must arrive. A MySQL logical message is not one Ethernet/TCP packet.

rds.flow: Application → chosen writer/read endpoint → SQL result; replication and historical recovery are separate paths.

dynamodb.name: DynamoDB scaling & recovery
dynamodb.role: Operate a managed key-value database by access pattern, partition pressure and recovery policy.
bullets: On-demand manages request capacity; provisioned mode uses configured RCU/WCU with optional Auto Scaling. Auto Scaling reacts to usage and is not instantaneous.

A hot partition key can throttle even when table totals appear low. Inspect throttling reason, key distribution and GSI capacity; a GSI with insufficient write capacity can back-pressure table writes.
DAX accelerates supported eventually consistent reads with a compatible client; strong reads bypass its cache to DynamoDB. Global tables replicate across Regions; they do not provide historical undo.
Enable PITR for supported continuous recovery and use on-demand/AWS Backup snapshots for retention requirements. Restore produces a new table; recheck dependent settings and application routing.
dynamodb.boundary: Variable unpredictable traffic → consider on-demand; predictable demand → provisioned plus scaling. Correct hot keys before blindly increasing total capacity.
dynamodb.investigate: Inspect consumed/provisioned capacity, throttles by table/index, latency, failed conditions and Contributor Insights hot-key evidence where enabled.
dynamodb.remediate: Adjust capacity or access pattern, verify per-key success and tail latency; test restore and switch the application to the validated new table.
dynamodb.example:
aws dynamodb describe-continuous-backups --table-name Orders
aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name Orders
dynamodb.trigger: Throttles despite low aggregate utilisation → inspect partitions/indexes, not only table totals.
dynamodb.trap: TTL deletion is asynchronous; it is not a precise scheduler. Replication does not preserve every previous valid value.
dynamodb.analogy: A warehouse can have free space overall while one busy loading bay is overloaded.
dynamodb.flow: Key-based request → table / index capacity → result; recovery creates a new table.

cache.name: ElastiCache & cache operations
cache.role: Reduce repeated database work while managing freshness, eviction and failure behaviour.
bullets: Valkey/Redis OSS shards partition data; replicas copy their shard asynchronously and support reads/failover in suitable configurations. More replicas do not spread primary writes across shards.

Node-based Memcached provides a simpler distributed cache without Redis OSS-style primary/replica failover. Serverless and node-based models differ in scaling, controls and pricing; inspect the chosen deployment model.

Cache-aside populates on a miss; TTL expires entries without refreshing them. Write-through updates database/cache in a coordinated application workflow; invalidation removes the cached value after a database change.
Track hit rate, evictions, memory, engine CPU, connections and replication lag. A cache outage can suddenly push the entire read load onto the database.
cache.boundary: HTTP objects at the edge → CloudFront; DynamoDB-compatible cache → DAX; custom sessions/computed values → ElastiCache.
cache.investigate: Check whether misses, hot keys, memory pressure or a node failure preceded database load. Compare DB and cached values before assuming a stale response is a DB issue.
cache.remediate: Tune TTL/invalidation, memory or shard capacity; test failover and cold-cache load. Use bounded retries and protect the source database.
cache.example:
# Cache-aside pseudocode
value = cache.get("product:42")
if value is None:
    value = database.read(42)
    cache.set("product:42", value, ttl=60)
cache.trigger: Read-heavy repeated values with acceptable staleness → caching; write pressure → examine shards and workload, not just replicas.
cache.trap: TTL expiration does not refresh data, and database/cache writes are not automatically atomic.
cache.analogy: A desk copy saves trips to the archive, but someone must decide when that copy is too old.
cache.flow: Read → cache hit, or miss → database → cache population; write/invalidation follows the selected strategy.

backup.name: AWS Backup & disaster recovery
backup.role: Schedule protected recovery points, manage retention/copies and prove that recovery works.
bullets: Backup plans select resources by explicit assignment or tags; check roles, supported resource settings and job outcomes. Copy to another account/Region when the recovery requirement calls for it.
Vault Lock protects retention with governance/compliance semantics; compliance mode becomes immutable after its grace period. Choose deliberately before committing retention controls.
Restore testing exercises supported restores and validation. An available recovery point says little about application readiness, permissions, dependencies or actual RTO.
Backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby and active/active trade ongoing cost against recovery work. RTO is tolerable outage; RPO is tolerable lost time of data. Both require measurement.
backup.boundary: Choose the least costly tested procedure that meets both objectives; replication/failover handles availability but can replicate corruption.
backup.investigate: Inspect backup/copy/restore job status, last recoverable timestamp, vault/account/Region, encryption grants, retention and application dependency order.
backup.remediate: Restore into isolation, validate business records and integrations, time the full cutover and clean up test resources. Record the demonstrated RTO/RPO.
backup.example:
aws backup list-backup-jobs --by-state FAILED
aws backup list-recovery-points-by-backup-vault --backup-vault-name orders-vault
backup.trigger: Keep recoverable history outside the workload account → controlled cross-account backup copies and tested access.
backup.trap: Replication is not a backup. No universal RTO belongs to a DR label; recovery time depends on the actual tested procedure.
backup.analogy: A spare building is useful only if the recovery team has the keys and has practised opening it.
backup.flow: Protected resource → recovery point → optional copy → restore → application/data validation.

cfn.name: CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle
cfn.role: Maintain declared resources through reviewed stack changes and controlled failure recovery.
bullets: CDK synthesises templates and assets; CloudFormation provisions the stack. Change sets preview supported changes and replacements; they do not guarantee an update will succeed.

Read stack events from the first relevant failure. UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED requires repairing the rollback cause and continuing rollback. Skipping resources is a last resort and leaves reconciliation work.

Drift detection compares supported resource properties to the template; it does not automatically repair drift or inspect every property. DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy protect different deletion/replacement moments.

StackSets distribute stacks across accounts/Regions with permissions, concurrency and failure-tolerance controls. Parameters are inputs; conditions choose resources/properties; DependsOn orders dependencies.
cfn.boundary: Need repeatable infrastructure → a stack; preview a change → change set; distribute the template → StackSets; share an existing supported resource → RAM.
cfn.investigate: Inspect resource status reason, service role, quotas, subnet IP capacity, name collisions, missing exports and replacement dependencies. Distinguish update failure from rollback failure.
cfn.remediate: Fix the prerequisite, continue rollback where appropriate, review the next change set and verify stack status plus application health. Reconcile any skipped resource before another update.
cfn.example:
aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --stack-name orders
# After fixing the specific rollback cause:
aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback --stack-name orders
cfn.trigger: Stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED → fix cause, then continue-update-rollback.
cfn.trap: Deleting a failed production stack is not a routine recovery step. A change set is a preview, not an executed deployment.
cfn.analogy: The template is the agreed building plan; drift is a room changed outside that plan.

notes.title: IAM, stack policy, termination protection or Retain?
notes.flow: Caller IAM → UpdateStack → separate stack-policy check → resource changes / failure
paragraphs: A stack policy is a separate JSON document attached to the stack. It restricts updates to existing logical resources even when IAM permits UpdateStack. Update:Modify, Update:Replace and Update:Delete describe update actions; Update:* covers all three.

A prohibited change fails the update; CloudFormation does not silently skip it and report success. An authorised operator can supply a temporary override for an intentional protected update. Other resources may already have changed before a later permission failure; rollback can fail or be disabled.
notes.trigger: Protect a database during stack updates → stack policy; first identify which operation must be blocked.
notes.trap: A stack policy is neither an IAM permission grant nor protection against direct service API calls.

rows: Block deletion of the entire stack
Keep a resource when deleting its stack

notes.title: Regional stacks, account-wide names
notes.flow:
Sydney stack creates a named IAM role → another Region tries the same name → conflict
Alternative: generate a unique name OR explicitly reference the one owned resource
paragraphs: IAM role/user names are account-wide, not shared across every AWS account. CloudFormation stacks are Regional: a second stack does not silently adopt an existing role with the same RoleName.
Omit optional physical names, or include Region/stack identifiers. Intentional sharing needs one owner and an ARN input/reference; importing a resource is a separate explicit workflow.

S3 buckets are Regional too, but traditional general-purpose bucket names share a namespace across accounts/Regions within a partition. Current S3 also supports optional account-Regional namespaces with a prescribed name suffix.
notes.trigger: Same template fails only in the second Region with AlreadyExists → check account-wide physical names.
notes.trap: Referencing an ARN does not create a second resource. A late create failure does not prove earlier resources were never created.
notes.example:
# Template excerpt for a NEW role, not a reference to an existing role
RoleName: !Sub "${AWS::StackName}-${AWS::Region}-app"
# For intentional reuse, take an ExistingRoleArn parameter instead.

cfn.flow: Template (optionally CDK synthesis) → reviewed stack operation → resource events → health verification.

images.name: Images & deployment operations
images.role: Promote tested machine/container artifacts and update an existing deployment safely.
bullets: EC2 Image Builder automates build, test and distribution of AMIs/container images. An AMI is regional; copying encrypted images requires compatible KMS permissions.
ECR stores images; ECS/EKS run containers. Check image URI/digest, pull permissions, platform architecture, registry connectivity, task/pod events, probes and resource limits.
Use immutable digests for repeatable releases. Rolling changes existing capacity in batches; blue/green retains another environment during cutover. Account for database compatibility and rollback.
Git records changes; Terraform plans/applies its managed resources with protected remote state and locking. Avoid two IaC tools independently owning the same resource.
images.boundary: Image creation/distribution → Image Builder/ECR; workload rollout → the existing ASG/ECS/EKS/deployment service. Operate the chosen pipeline rather than redesigning one for this exam.
images.investigate: For failed deployment, start at events and the first unhealthy dependency: subnet IP exhaustion, image pull, permissions, startup command, health probe or application config.
images.remediate: Correct the dependency and redeploy a pinned artifact with a controlled rollout; verify new revision, healthy count, error rate and rollback readiness.
images.example:
aws ecs describe-services --cluster orders --services orders-api
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name orders-api
images.trigger: Same fault on every replacement instance → investigate the image/template/config, not repeated manual instance repair.
images.trap: An uploaded image is not a running task. A mutable latest tag makes rollback provenance harder to prove.
images.analogy: The image is a sealed installation kit; deployment decides where and when that kit runs.

notes.title: AMI ≠ working disk ≠ Launch Template
notes.flow:
Working EBS → snapshot
AMI = boot metadata + snapshot references
Launch Template = AMI ID + instance/network/storage settings
Launch → fresh EBS volumes from snapshots → new instance
paragraphs: Boot metadata includes architecture, root-device mappings, virtualisation type and boot mode. An EBS-backed AMI refers to snapshots; it is not the live volume still attached to the source instance.

ASG launches normally create new root volumes from the image’s snapshots. Reattaching an existing data disk is a different explicit workflow. A replacement AMI can be created from a running/stopped instance or a suitable retained root snapshot with matching boot settings.
notes.trigger: Need repeatable replacement instances → usable image plus launch configuration, not a plan to move one root disk between every launch.
notes.trap: A snapshot is disk data; it does not alone specify every boot setting or the desired EC2 instance type.

notes.title: Image consistency and deregistration recovery
notes.flow:
Coordinate application writes → flush/freeze or allow reboot → capture image → test boot AND data
Deregistered AMI → matching pre-existing Recycle Bin rule? → restore within retention
paragraphs: Durable captured blocks do not automatically prove application consistency. Allowing the image-creation reboot helps flush buffered state; transactional applications can need their own quiesce/backup coordination. “Disable No reboot” means allow reboot.

An accidentally deregistered eligible EBS-backed AMI can be recovered through Recycle Bin when a matching retention rule already applied and retention has not expired. Otherwise investigate retained snapshots or a surviving instance; reconstruct with correct boot settings.
notes.trigger: Before-image consistency requirements and recoverable historical artifacts change the recovery answer.
notes.trap: “Deregistered means never recoverable” is outdated. A retention rule created after the deletion does not retroactively save an unretained image.

notes.title: AZ, account and Region are separate sharing boundaries
notes.flow:
Another AZ: same Regional AMI
Another account: AMI launch permission + eligible encryption access
Another Region: copy image, then share/use the destination copy
paragraphs: Sharing the AMI permits use of its backing snapshots for launching without separately sharing those snapshots. Copying a shared AMI can require additional read permissions for its backing storage.

Encrypted sharing needs a customer-managed KMS key with suitable cross-account permissions. An image encrypted under the default AWS-managed aws/ebs key cannot simply be shared cross-account. Copy/re-encrypt under an appropriate customer-managed key when required.

Another account and Region involves both sharing/access permissions and a destination-Region copy. Same-account cross-Region copying is not prohibited merely because the source used the AWS-managed aws/ebs key; use an appropriate destination-Region encryption key.
A KMS multi-Region key has distinct Regional primary/replica resources. Ordinary customer-managed keys are not global, and Region copying is a separate boundary from cross-account key sharing.
notes.trigger: Launching a shared image and copying it have different backing-snapshot permission requirements.
notes.trap: Cross-account use does not imply cross-Region copying; name the changed boundary first.

notes.title: Baked agent: installed is not sending
notes.flow: AMI with agent/config → fresh instance → automatic startup + IAM + endpoints → telemetry
paragraphs: The image supplies the installed CloudWatch Agent and configuration to each launch. ASG does not independently install software merely because it launches the AMI.

Publishing still needs startup, a valid instance role, correct configuration/dimensions and endpoint access. Validate a new instance’s own log/metric stream, not only the old source instance’s telemetry.
notes.trigger: Agent baked into image but new instance has no guest metrics → check startup, permissions and connectivity.
notes.trap: EC2 basic metrics can exist while memory/disk-space or application logs are missing.
notes.example:
# Linux diagnostic example
systemctl status amazon-cloudwatch-agent
# Check agent logs, instance-role permissions and HTTPS endpoint reachability.

images.flow: Build → test → registry / AMI distribution → controlled rollout → health gate.

ssm.name: Systems Manager operations
ssm.role: Inventory, connect to, patch, configure and automate managed resources.
bullets: Managed nodes need an agent where applicable, instance/service permissions and network connectivity. Session Manager avoids opening inbound SSH/RDP; configure session logging and access explicitly.

Run Command performs supported commands; Automation runbooks coordinate operational steps/API calls with optional approvals. State Manager maintains desired associations; Patch Manager handles patch baselines/operations.
Maintenance Windows schedule controlled maintenance. Parameter Store holds configuration and SecureString values; Secrets Manager adds supported secret rotation workflows.
Limit automation concurrency and error thresholds. Multi-account/Region execution needs trusted roles and target access; an automation service role is separate from a node’s role.
ssm.boundary: One command on managed nodes → Run Command; a repair procedure with branching/approval → Automation; ongoing desired setup → State Manager.
ssm.investigate: For an offline node, inspect agent service/version, instance role, DNS/proxy, time, and outbound HTTPS to required endpoints. No inbound SSH rule is required for Session Manager.
ssm.remediate: Restore management connectivity, target a safe tag group, dry-run/test where supported, then verify command/runbook output and actual service health.
ssm.example:
aws ssm describe-instance-information
# Example runbook; review its steps and target before execution
aws ssm start-automation-execution --document-name AWS-RestartEC2Instance \
  --parameters InstanceId=i-0123456789abcdef0
ssm.trigger: Repeat a repair with approvals and auditability → Automation runbook.
ssm.trap: The console showing a node does not prove it is currently online. A successful command exit code is not an application health test.
ssm.analogy: A managed workshop: access, tool inventory, maintenance schedule and repeatable repair instructions.

notes.title: Agent management versus offline EC2Rescue
notes.flow:
Online: agent + node IAM + outbound HTTPS → SSM
Offline rescue: Automation → temporary helper → detached root EBS → repair → reattach
paragraphs: Ordinary agent-based management requires a working agent, credentials/permissions and outbound endpoint connectivity. Automation is broader: its runbooks can call AWS APIs without executing inside the impaired OS.

AWSSupport-ExecuteEC2Rescue can orchestrate an offline workflow using temporary helper resources and the impaired instance’s root EBS volume. Review the runbook’s prerequisites, permissions, backup and stop/restart behaviour. This is not an agent command somehow running inside an unreachable OS.
Use repair when preserving/fixing this instance matters. An ASG generally replaces an unhealthy instance; guard against that replacement interfering with intentional repair or maintenance.
notes.trigger: Agent unreachable and root-volume repair required → appropriate offline rescue runbook, not repeated Run Command.
notes.trap: An installed agent is not evidence it is currently running or connected.

ssm.flow: Authorised operator / event → runbook → scoped API or managed-node operation → recorded outcome.

accounts.name: Multi-account operations
accounts.role: Apply approved governance and share or deploy resources across account and Region boundaries.
bullets: Organizations organises accounts/OUs; SCPs restrict applicable member-account permissions and never grant access. IAM Identity Center provides workforce federation and permission-set access.
Control Tower establishes/governs a landing zone; Service Catalog distributes approved products. RAM shares supported existing resources, such as subnets, without cloning every resource.
StackSets deploys template instances; regional settings and service availability still matter. Track execution roles, delegated administration, organisational units and excluded accounts.

Use tags, Cost Explorer and Cost and Usage Reports to identify waste and ownership; check Compute Optimizer/Trusted Advisor recommendations against workload requirements. Savings Plans are discounts, not capacity guarantees.
accounts.boundary: Replicate infrastructure → StackSets; share a resource → RAM; limit allowed operations → SCP; grant a workforce session → Identity Center plus permission policies.
accounts.investigate: When one account fails, compare OU/SCP inheritance, role trust, service-linked roles, Region enablement, quotas and target resource policies.
accounts.remediate: Repair the smallest applicable control, test with a least-privilege session and verify both allowed and intentionally denied operations across the affected accounts.
accounts.example:
aws cloudformation list-stack-instances --stack-set-name baseline
aws organizations list-policies-for-target --target-id ACCOUNT_ID \
  --filter SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY
accounts.trigger: Same baseline in many accounts/Regions → StackSets; share existing subnets → RAM.
accounts.trap: An SCP allow does not grant an IAM permission. Cost optimisation must preserve availability and recovery constraints.
accounts.analogy: Account policies set the building rules; IAM grants individual access cards.

notes.title: StackSets: one template, separate target stacks
notes.flow: Common template → StackSet → selected account × Region stacks → per-target status
paragraphs: Each selected account–Region combination receives its own stack/resources. Region order and account concurrency control rollout; console, CLI/API and IaC can configure it.

StackSets replicate one template definition, with supported parameter overrides. They are not a general dependency orchestrator for unrelated templates. Check target roles, capabilities and resource naming before broad rollout.
notes.trigger: Apply the same baseline to many account–Region targets → StackSets.
notes.trap: A single StackSet operation does not create one global stack or one shared copy of every resource.

accounts.flow: Baseline → StackSet instances; existing supported resource → RAM share; access → IAM plus guardrails.

iam.name: IAM access investigation
iam.role: Separate authentication, role trust and permission to perform an action on a resource.
bullets: Identity policies grant actions to identities; resource policies grant supported resource access. Trust policies control role assumption. Cross-account access generally needs trust/resource permission and caller-side permission as applicable.

Explicit deny wins. Permissions boundaries, session policies and SCPs limit permissions; they do not independently grant them. Resource-policy evaluation has principal-specific exceptions: inspect the actual principal/session.

Use roles with temporary credentials and MFA/federation for people. IAM Access Analyzer identifies supported external/unused access; the policy simulator helps test policies but is not a full live request.
Inspect conditions such as source ARN/account, requested Region, tags, VPC endpoint and MFA. A valid credential does not bypass a missing network route.
iam.boundary: Cannot assume role → check caller permission and target trust; session exists but action denied → inspect action/resource, limits, conditions and relevant resource policy.
iam.investigate: Start with sts get-caller-identity, exact denied action/resource and CloudTrail error. Decode an encoded authorisation message with STS when present and authorised.
iam.remediate: Correct narrowly scoped policies, then retry the precise operation and test a prohibited operation. Avoid attaching AdministratorAccess as an investigation shortcut.
iam.example:
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws sts decode-authorization-message --encoded-message ENCODED_MESSAGE
# Requires sts:DecodeAuthorizationMessage; inspect returned decision context.
iam.trigger: A user authenticated successfully yet receives AccessDenied → investigate authorisation, not a password reset.
iam.trap: An execution role controls what code calls; it does not automatically allow a service to invoke that code. A network filter cannot grant IAM access.
iam.analogy: Trust admits a visitor; permissions specify rooms; guardrails limit the entire visit.

notes.title: Cross-account S3 copy: keep one identity with both permissions
notes.flow:
Finance credentials → CopyObject(destination Finance, source HR/Audit)
Same credentials must pass source GetObject AND destination PutObject
paragraphs: Direct access can combine Finance identity-policy permissions with HR/Audit bucket policies granting the Finance principal source reads. Identity policies attach to users/groups/roles; bucket policies attach to buckets.

AssumeRole returns a different role session. It does not union the original Finance user’s permissions with the HR role’s permissions. A role needs trust for assumption and permissions for the actual source/destination operations.
This example assumes same-partition general-purpose buckets and isolates policy evaluation. Object ownership, explicit denies, organisation controls and any SSE-KMS permissions can add requirements.
notes.trigger: Copy across accounts while retaining existing Finance writes → grant direct source access to that Finance identity.
notes.trap: Assuming a source-account role does not automatically carry the original identity’s destination write permission.
notes.example:
# Excerpt: run with the intended Finance profile; review all policies first
aws s3api copy-object --profile finance --bucket finance-archive \
  --key audit/report.csv --copy-source audit-source/report.csv

iam.flow: Principal → trusted session → action/resource/context evaluation → allowed or denied operation.

config.name: Config & continuous compliance
config.role: Record supported resource configuration changes and evaluate configured compliance rules.
bullets: A recorder captures supported resource types in its configured scope; rules evaluate recorded configuration or periodic conditions. An aggregator collects multi-account/Region views; it does not replace source recorders.
Conformance packs group rules and remediation definitions. Automatic remediation requires configured permissions and safe assumptions; stale evaluations can trigger inappropriate action.
CloudTrail records the API actor, while Config records the resource’s configuration history. Artifact supplies AWS compliance documents, not continuous auditing of your workload.
Implement supplied classification and compliance requirements through tags, resource selection, encryption and approved Regions/services; do not invent the organisation’s policy.
config.boundary: Need history/compliance of a resource property → Config; need who changed it → CloudTrail.
config.investigate: Check recorder status, resource support/scope, delivery errors, rule triggers, evaluation timestamp and remediation execution output.
config.remediate: Correct the resource through managed configuration, re-evaluate and verify COMPLIANT plus the actual setting. Adjust permissions/preconditions to prevent remediation loops.
config.example:
aws configservice describe-compliance-by-config-rule \
  --compliance-types NON_COMPLIANT
aws configservice describe-configuration-recorder-status
config.trigger: Continuously identify unencrypted supported resources → Config rule/conformance pack.
config.trap: An aggregator is a view, not automatic recording or repair. A compliant rule result only proves that rule’s evaluated condition.
config.analogy: A property inspection log, compared with a checklist at each relevant change.
config.flow: Supported resource configuration → recorder → rule evaluation → safe remediation → re-evaluation.

kms.name: KMS, encryption & secrets
kms.role: Control cryptographic key use separately from access to encrypted data.
bullets: SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys; SSE-KMS uses KMS-protected data keys. A customer-managed KMS key offers policy/lifecycle control. SSE-C supplies a key to S3 over HTTPS; client-side encryption happens before upload.

Envelope encryption protects large data locally with a data key; KMS protects that key. GenerateDataKey returns plaintext and encrypted representations; the application stores the encrypted one and protects/clears plaintext.

A KMS key policy is essential; IAM permission only works when the key policy permits that mechanism. Cross-account key use needs appropriate key-policy and identity permissions. Check key Region, state, grants and encryption context.
Secrets Manager stores and rotates supported credentials; Parameter Store SecureString protects named configuration. Rotation must update dependent applications and connectivity correctly.
kms.boundary: Object read allowed but SSE-KMS decryption denied → check key access as well as S3. Key rotation does not require re-encrypting every object and does not fix an access policy.
kms.investigate: Inspect the exact KMS error, CloudTrail key operation, key ARN/state, key policy, caller IAM policy, grants and encryption context. A disabled/deleting key can make data unavailable.
kms.remediate: Restore approved key access/state, retry a controlled decrypt/read and verify expected denies. Test a rotated secret with the dependent service before marking rotation complete.
kms.example:
aws kms describe-key --key-id KEY_ARN
aws kms get-key-policy --key-id KEY_ARN --policy-name default
# Inspect policy; do not print secrets or plaintext data keys into logs.
kms.trigger: S3 GetObject permission succeeds but encrypted object remains unreadable → KMS policy/state/context investigation.
kms.trap: KMS permissions do not grant S3 access; S3 permissions do not automatically grant KMS use. GenerateDataKeyWithPlaintext is not an API.
kms.analogy: Access to the locked cabinet and permission to use its key are separate checks.

rows: S3 permissions and resulting object mode.
Object access plus applicable KMS policy/state/context.
Customer sends key over HTTPS; S3 encrypts
Customer retains key; S3 does not persist it; no inherent KMS dependency.
Client key recovery/libraries; S3 receives ciphertext.

notes.title: Encrypted ASG launches: authorise the service-linked role
notes.flow:
AMI + encrypted snapshot → ASG service-linked role → KMS authorisation → fresh encrypted volume
Application instance profile acts later, after the instance boots.
paragraphs: For a customer-managed key in the ASG account, grant the ASG service-linked role the documented key-use and grant-creation permissions. Giving only the instance application role decrypt access does not authorise image launch.

For a key owned by another account, AWS’s ASG workflow requires the key policy plus an explicit KMS grant for the ASG service-linked role. An authorised principal creates that grant; this is not a cross-account AssumeRole flow.

Copying/re-encrypting the image under a key in the consuming account is an alternative, not mandatory. A question that omits key ownership is missing the deciding condition; do not silently assume another account.

A missing launch-key permission can surface as generic Client.InternalError. Check the ASG service-linked role (normally AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling), source key ownership and scaling activity. EC2/EBS creates a new virtual volume; data keys encrypt blocks and KMS keys protect those data keys. Exact KMS operations depend on source-snapshot encryption.
notes.trigger: Encrypted ASG launch fails before application startup → inspect the service-linked role, key owner, policy and required grant.
notes.trap: A role trust policy, an application-role Allow and a KMS grant are different controls.

docs.label: AWS ASG key policy and grant examples

rows: Documented key policy for ASG service-linked role
Key policy + explicit grant for ASG service-linked role
AssumeRole alone or AMI launch permission alone

kms.flow: Encrypted data key → authorised KMS Decrypt → recovered data key → local/service data decryption.

certs.name: ACM & encrypted connections
certs.role: Maintain trusted certificates and TLS configuration at the actual termination point.
bullets: ALB HTTPS listeners need a suitable certificate in the load balancer’s Region. A CloudFront viewer certificate from ACM must be in us-east-1.
Check SAN/hostname match, expiry, validation status, chain and listener security policy. Eligible ACM-managed renewal relies on continued validation and service use.
Viewer-to-edge TLS and edge/load-balancer-to-origin TLS are separate connections. Encrypting one leg does not prove the backend leg is protected.
certs.boundary: Need certificate lifecycle → ACM; need encryption keys for stored data → KMS. DNS validation proves domain control, not application health.
certs.investigate: Inspect the certificate actually served with SNI, DNS record, listener binding, validation records and origin hostname/trust.
certs.remediate: Attach/renew the correct certificate and policy, then test hostname validation and both connection legs. Retain DNS validation records for managed renewal.
certs.example:
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null
# Diagnostic command; inspect certificate dates, chain and hostname separately.
certs.trigger: Browser certificate mismatch → hostname/certificate/listener investigation before changing IAM.
certs.trap: A valid certificate in the wrong Region cannot be attached to the ALB. CloudFront’s viewer certificate Region is a special requirement.
certs.analogy: A certificate is a verified identity document for a particular connection endpoint.
certs.flow: Domain validation → suitable ACM certificate → correct listener/endpoint → validated TLS connection.

findings.name: Security findings & classification
findings.role: Interpret the finding type, prioritise impact and verify the relevant corrective control.
bullets: GuardDuty detects threats from supported data sources; Inspector assesses supported workload vulnerabilities/exposure; Macie discovers sensitive S3 data.

Security Hub aggregates/prioritises supported findings and security posture checks. Config evaluates configuration compliance. Trusted Advisor provides supported advisory checks; availability depends on plan/feature.
Apply the supplied data classification to access, encryption, retention and logging. A classification label without enforcement does not protect data.

Current guide terminology includes AWS Security Agent; its docs now describe it as part of AWS Continuum. It supports application security review/threat modelling/penetration testing, not a replacement for runtime threat detection.
findings.boundary: Vulnerable package → Inspector; suspicious activity → GuardDuty; sensitive S3 content → Macie; aggregate findings → Security Hub.
findings.investigate: Read resource/account/Region, evidence, severity, last observation and workflow status. Confirm the affected running artifact and possible exposure before dismissing a finding.
findings.remediate: Patch/isolate/restrict according to the approved runbook; rescan and verify runtime version, connectivity and finding state. Preserve investigation evidence.
findings.example:
# Inspector example: list findings for inspection, then filter to the affected resource
aws inspector2 list-findings --max-results 10
findings.trigger: Central view of findings from several supported security services → Security Hub.
findings.trap: A suppressed or archived finding is not proof of remediation. AWS Artifact reports describe AWS controls, not your instance’s patch status.
findings.analogy: Different inspectors check different hazards; the central register does not perform every inspection.
findings.flow: Specialist assessment → finding → prioritised investigation → corrective control → reassessment.

vpc.name: VPC routes, subnets & filters
vpc.role: Provide address space, routing and traffic controls for VPC-associated workloads.
bullets: A VPC is regional; a subnet belongs to one AZ. Plan non-overlapping CIDRs, free subnet IPs and routes. A public subnet has an internet-gateway route; an instance also needs appropriate addressing and filters for IPv4 internet access.
Route tables select paths; longest-prefix matching matters. Security groups are stateful allow filters on ENIs; NACLs are stateless ordered allow/deny filters at subnet boundaries.

IPv4 private egress commonly uses NAT; an egress-only internet gateway handles outbound-initiated IPv6 internet connections. For zonal NAT deployments, align AZ paths to avoid a dependency on another AZ and unnecessary transfer.

Peering is non-transitive and needs routes on both sides. Transit Gateway connects supported networks through attachments and associated/propagated route tables. These paths still need security controls.
vpc.boundary: An IAM denial needs policy analysis; a timeout needs DNS/routes/filters/target checks. A route does not grant application authorisation.
vpc.investigate: Trace DNS → source subnet route → gateway/attachment → destination route → SG/NACL → listener → return path. Check overlapping CIDRs and subnet address exhaustion.
vpc.remediate: Correct the specific route/filter/address issue, test from the affected source and verify both request and response. Restrict the fix to required peers/ports.
vpc.example:
# Return path illustration, not firewall syntax
browser:54321 → ALB:443
ALB:443 → browser:54321
# NACLs must permit the relevant destination ports in both directions.
vpc.trigger: Request arrives but response is blocked with stateless filtering → inspect ephemeral return-port rules.
vpc.trap: A NAT gateway does not accept unsolicited inbound internet connections. An internet-gateway route alone does not assign a public IP.
vpc.analogy: Routes are roads; firewalls are gates; DNS is the address book.

rows: Explicit request and ephemeral return rules.
Destination must have a valid return route too.
A correct answer does not prove TCP connectivity.

notes.title: Same VPC: a route is not permission
notes.flow:
App ENI → subnet route table’s local path → DB ENI
                      then applicable SG / NACL checks → database port
paragraphs: A VPC is Regional; a subnet occupies one AZ. Each subnet has one associated route table, while a table can serve several subnets. Tables automatically have local routes for the VPC CIDRs; separate same-VPC subnets normally already have a routing path.

That path does not authorise the connection. A typical EC2 → RDS connection needs the DB security group to allow the database port from the app security group, plus permitted NACL/return traffic. SGs apply to ENIs/resources; NACLs apply at subnet boundaries.
IPv4 and IPv6 CIDRs are separate address spaces. IPv6 assignment is optional; an EC2 instance does not automatically receive IPv6 merely because it exists in a VPC.
notes.trigger: Same-VPC SQL timeout with a valid local route → check DB ingress, NACLs and the listener before adding routing infrastructure.
notes.trap: Different subnets do not, by themselves, mean private instances or blocked inter-subnet routing.

notes.title: New versus default security controls
