notes.flow: Route exists → verify the actual rules → test request AND return traffic
paragraphs: These are initial defaults, not a substitute for inspecting the current configuration. The default security group’s self-reference covers resources assigned to that group; it is not a blanket inbound allow from the whole VPC.
notes.trigger: A newly created custom NACL can block a routed connection before any application code runs.
notes.trap: “Default security group” and “new custom security group” have different initial inbound rules.

notes.title: IGW, NAT and egress-only IGW
notes.flow:
Direct IPv4: public IPv4/EIP + IGW route + filters
Private IPv4: private instance → public NAT → IGW
Outbound-only IPv6: IPv6 instance → egress-only IGW
paragraphs: For direct IPv4 internet access, an IGW route alone is insufficient: the instance also needs public IPv4 addressing and suitable rules. A public NAT gateway lets private IPv4 clients initiate connections and receive replies.
An egress-only IGW is IPv6-only: it permits outbound-initiated flows and their replies while preventing new internet-initiated connections. It does not translate IPv4 or assign IPv6 addresses.
notes.trigger: Outbound-only IPv6 requirement → egress-only IGW; private IPv4 egress → suitable NAT path.
notes.trap: A public subnet route does not automatically attach a public address to every instance.

notes.title: Public address does not prove public-internet transit
notes.flow:
AWS public IP → AWS global network → AWS public IP (documented exceptions)
Private IP + configured peering routes → private-address path
paragraphs: Current AWS documentation says AWS-originating/AWS-destined public-IP traffic stays on its global network, except traffic to/from China Regions and the European Sovereign Cloud Region.

Inter-Region peering supplies private addressing/routes over the AWS backbone. Merely creating peering does not reroute calls still addressed to public IPs. Routes, permissions, addressing and TLS remain separate checks.
notes.trigger: Need private addressing → private connectivity/routes; do not use an outdated public-IP transit explanation.
notes.trap: Edge locations and Direct Connect are not automatically inserted into an ordinary EC2-to-EC2 request.

vpc.flow: Source → route → applicable filters → target listener → permitted return path.

callout.title: Subnet IPs · 5 reserved addresses
callout.text: In a standard IPv4 subnet, AWS reserves the first four addresses and the last address. Example: 10.0.0.0/24 has 256 − 5 = 251 assignable addresses.
callout.note: The DNS resolver is at primary VPC CIDR + 2; every subnet’s +2 is still reserved. BYOIP has exceptions. Standard IPv6 subnets also reserve the first four and last address.

endpoints.name: Endpoints & private connectivity
endpoints.role: Reach supported services privately with the correct endpoint and DNS/routing model.
bullets: Gateway endpoints support S3 and DynamoDB using route-table entries and service prefix lists; they do not create application-subnet ENIs and have no additional endpoint charge.
Interface endpoints use PrivateLink ENIs in selected subnets/AZs with security groups and optional private DNS. They typically charge hourly and for data processing.
An endpoint policy limits applicable access; it does not replace IAM, resource or KMS policies. S3 supports gateway and interface models with different reachability/use cases.

Troubleshoot existing Site-to-Site VPN/Client VPN and hybrid routes with tunnel status, BGP/static routes, DNS forwarding and filters. Consider Transit Gateway/peering path and return routing; do not assume transitive peering.
endpoints.boundary: Private EC2 to S3/DynamoDB in the same Region/VPC context → gateway endpoint is often sufficient; supported private API access via ENIs → interface endpoint.
endpoints.investigate: Check service/Region, private DNS, VPC DNS settings, endpoint SG:443, route-table association, endpoint policy and caller/resource permissions.
endpoints.remediate: Correct routing/DNS/access, test the service API from the private workload and confirm the actual endpoint path. Compare endpoint and NAT costs for traffic volume and AZ placement.
endpoints.example:
aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0123456789abcdef0
# Gateway: S3 prefix-list route; interface: HTTPS → private ENI.
endpoints.trigger: No NAT needed for private S3 access from the workload VPC → suitable S3 gateway endpoint.
endpoints.trap: Gateway endpoints are not transitive through peering/TGW for remote clients. Registering an endpoint does not authorise every API operation.
endpoints.analogy: A private doorway still needs a working road, the correct address and an access card.

rows: S3/DynamoDB; no additional endpoint charge; not a transitive hybrid doorway.
PrivateLink ENIs + SGs in selected subnets
Supported APIs/private DNS; hourly and processing charges.

endpoints.flow: Signed service request → gateway route or interface ENI → AWS service; permissions remain separate.

dns.name: Route 53 & DNS operations
dns.role: Resolve names and choose DNS answers according to the configured routing and health policy.
bullets: Public hosted zones answer internet DNS; private hosted zones require appropriate VPC association/resolution. Check delegation, record type/name and split-horizon behaviour.

Failover supports primary/secondary answers; weighted splits DNS answers; latency selects suitable regional endpoints. Health checks and EvaluateTargetHealth affect eligible answers, subject to policy behaviour.

Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints and forwarding rules support hybrid name resolution. Allow DNS traffic and avoid forwarding loops; log queries to investigate actual names/responses. Current documentation calls the VPC service Route 53 VPC Resolver; the exam guide also uses the older Resolver name.
DNS Firewall filters supported Resolver queries by domain rules. WAF filters HTTP requests, Shield addresses DDoS protection and Network Firewall filters network traffic; their boundaries differ.
dns.boundary: Name fails but IP works → DNS investigation. Static global IP entry and supported endpoint failover → Global Accelerator may fit better than DNS changes.
dns.investigate: Use dig from the affected network; inspect authoritative answers, TTL/cache, hosted-zone association, Resolver rules, endpoint SGs and health-check results.
dns.remediate: Repair delegation/record/forwarding, then verify from public and private clients after appropriate cache expiry. DNS failover is not instant active-connection migration.
dns.example:
dig api.example.com
dig @VPC_RESOLVER_IP internal.example.com
# Use a real reachable resolver IP; compare answer, status and TTL.
dns.trigger: Only on-premises clients cannot resolve a private AWS name → inspect Resolver inbound path and conditional forwarding.
dns.trap: DNS supplies an address; the application request is a separate connection. Weighted DNS does not guarantee a precise per-request percentage.
dns.analogy: An address book can choose a branch, but it does not carry the visitor to that branch.
dns.flow: Name query → appropriate resolver/zone → routing policy → DNS answer; application traffic follows separately.

edge.name: CloudFront & Global Accelerator
edge.role: Operate global delivery with the right cache, origin and failover behaviour.
bullets: CloudFront caches eligible HTTP content at edge locations. Behaviours choose origins by path; a cache key distinguishes query strings/headers/cookies that genuinely change the response.

An origin group supplies primary/secondary failover for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS under configured failure conditions; it does not merge responses. TTL changes cannot fix a missing language/tenant cache-key dimension.
CloudFront Functions handles lightweight supported viewer transformations; Lambda@Edge supports broader request/response processing. Dynamic content alone does not require edge code.
Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP entry and routes supported TCP/UDP application traffic to healthy endpoints over the AWS network; it is not an HTTP object cache.
edge.boundary: Cache HTTP responses/static S3 images → CloudFront; stable global IPs and endpoint routing → Global Accelerator. Compare transfer, request, invalidation and accelerator charges.
edge.investigate: Inspect DNS, viewer/origin TLS, behaviour match, cache policy, origin request policy, status/error caching, origin health and relevant access/WAF logs.
edge.remediate: Correct the policy/origin rather than repeatedly lowering TTL; invalidate when appropriate, then test cache hit/miss and response correctness for distinct request variants.
edge.example:
# Conceptual cache keys
/reviews?lang=en → /reviews|lang=en
/reviews?lang=ja → /reviews|lang=ja
# Include lang in cache policy if it changes the origin response.
edge.trigger: Wrong language served from cache → cache key; need a stable global anycast entry → Global Accelerator.
edge.trap: Forwarding a parameter to the origin and including it in the cache key are distinct choices. Origin failover is not general write-request replay.
edge.analogy: CloudFront is a local copy desk; Global Accelerator is a globally advertised entrance to the application.

rows: Path-based HTTP content sources and caching
Treating every origin as a failover target.
Assuming general POST replay or merged responses.
Assuming dynamic content always requires edge code.
Static anycast entry + supported endpoint routing
Treating it as an HTTP object cache.

notes.title: Origin Shield consolidates cache misses
notes.flow:
Viewer → edge → Regional edge cache → selected Origin Shield → origin
                                (applicable bypass/routing exceptions)
paragraphs: Origin Shield is an additional AWS-managed CloudFront caching layer in a selected Region, not an ElastiCache cluster you deploy. It consolidates eligible origin-bound misses from caching layers.
Choose the supported Shield Region with the lowest latency to the origin. Weighted DNS can distribute traffic but does not inherently consolidate repeated misses or improve cache reuse.
notes.trigger: Many cache locations request the same uncached object → evaluate Origin Shield for origin-load reduction.
notes.trap: The typical cache hierarchy has exceptions; do not promise every request always traverses every cache layer.

notes.title: S3 REST origin versus website custom origin
notes.flow:
Preferred private origin: CloudFront OAC → signed S3 REST request → restrictive bucket policy
Website endpoint: CloudFront custom origin → HTTP website request
paragraphs: OAC is preferred over legacy OAI for supported S3 REST origins. S3 website endpoints are custom origins: neither OAC nor OAI applies, and the website endpoint supports HTTP only.

A configured secret Referer header checked by a bucket policy is a limited website-origin workaround. Headers can be spoofed; this is not equivalent to authenticated OAC access. For robust CloudFront-only access, use the REST endpoint with appropriate OAC and bucket restrictions.
notes.trigger: Private S3 content accessible only through a distribution → REST origin + OAC + scoped bucket policy.
notes.trap: Changing an origin label does not turn a website endpoint into a REST endpoint or add HTTPS support.

notes.title: Endpoint location versus SigV4 signing Region
notes.flow:
CloudFront (global) → request signed for Sydney
                         bucket now in Singapore → 400 AuthorizationHeaderMalformed
paragraphs: The origin endpoint directs the request; the SigV4 authorisation scope authenticates it and includes a Region. S3 must accept that signing Region. It is not merely a routing field in a JSON body.

Deleting a bucket and recreating its name in another Region can leave stale origin/signing information in a distribution. Confirm the actual bucket Region, update/re-save the CloudFront origin and allow deployment to finish, then retest.
CloudFront distributions are global and access keys do not have a home Region. An explicit wrong-Region S3 response proves an HTTP exchange occurred; it is different from a network timeout.
notes.trigger: S3 explicitly says the signing Region is wrong → investigate origin metadata and request scope, not CloudFront’s supposed home Region.
notes.trap: The bucket was deleted/recreated, not moved in place. Broader bucket permissions do not repair a malformed signing scope.
notes.example:
# Illustrative credential scope, not credentials or an executable request
Credential=<access-key-id>/<date>/ap-southeast-2/s3/aws4_request
# Compare the Region with what the actual S3 bucket expects.

edge.flow: Viewer → CloudFront cache hit or configured origin; Global Accelerator is an alternative traffic-entry pattern.

net-evidence.name: Network evidence & protection
net-evidence.role: Identify the failing hop with configuration analysis, flow records and measured network health.
bullets: VPC Flow Logs describe supported IP traffic metadata and ACCEPT/REJECT decisions; they are not packet payload captures and are not instantaneous.
Reachability Analyzer models supported configuration paths without sending packets. A reachable model does not prove the application is listening or healthy.

CloudWatch Internet Monitor observes internet-path performance for configured resources; Network Synthetic Monitor probes supported hybrid paths for latency/loss. Network Flow Monitor provides supported workload flow/performance visibility.

Use ALB/CloudFront access logs for HTTP status and timing, WAF logs for rule decisions and container logs for application/network startup faults. Audit WAF, Shield, DNS Firewall and Network Firewall at their own inspection boundaries.
net-evidence.boundary: Configuration block → Reachability Analyzer; actual accepted/rejected IP flow → Flow Logs; internet/hybrid degradation → the relevant CloudWatch network monitor.
net-evidence.investigate: Correlate source/destination IPs, ports, protocol, direction and time. Interpret ACCEPT as filter acceptance, not business success; verify route symmetry and DNS separately.
net-evidence.remediate: Repair the first proven failing dependency, retest actual connectivity/application response and compare before/after latency, loss and log outcomes.
net-evidence.example:
# Illustrative Flow Log excerpt, simplified
srcaddr=10.0.11.20 dstaddr=10.0.21.30 dstport=5432 protocol=6 action=REJECT
# Inspect relevant SG/NACL configuration; record alone does not identify the exact rule.
net-evidence.trigger: Need to locate a configured network block without probing production → Reachability Analyzer.
net-evidence.trap: Flow Logs ACCEPT is not HTTP 200. A trace gap can be sampling/instrumentation rather than a network failure.
net-evidence.analogy: A road map, a traffic register and a timed test drive answer different questions.
net-evidence.flow: Configuration model / flow record / live probe → evidence → targeted check → real traffic verification.

assistance.name: Health & assisted investigation
assistance.role: Use service health and assisted analysis as evidence within an accountable operational process.
bullets: AWS Health provides relevant service/account event information; compare affected Region/resources with your own telemetry rather than assuming every failure is AWS-wide.

AWS DevOps Agent correlates connected operational evidence and deployment context to investigate incidents and recommend improvements. Scope integrations/roles and validate conclusions against logs and metrics.
Kiro assists with code/configuration and troubleshooting workflows. Review generated commands and changes; an assistant recommendation is not a verified root cause or an approved production change.
Monitor AI workloads as workloads: access, model/API quotas, errors, latency, cost and sensitive logging. Bedrock being in scope does not turn SOA-C03 into model-training certification.
assistance.boundary: Suspected AWS service disruption → AWS Health plus resource telemetry; cross-signal investigation → assisted tooling with least-privilege evidence access.
assistance.investigate: Check the affected scope, linked telemetry, permissions and recent changes. Identify what evidence supports each hypothesis and what test would disprove it.
assistance.remediate: Execute the approved bounded repair, verify user-visible recovery and record evidence. Treat recommendations as inputs to change control, not automatic proof.
assistance.example:
# Investigation checklist (conceptual)
symptom → affected account/Region/AZ → evidence → hypothesis
→ approved action → user-visible verification → prevention
assistance.trigger: Current guide names Kiro/DevOps Agent: know their investigation/automation role, not an invented replacement for monitoring.
assistance.trap: The June 2026 guide revision matters; older SOA-C02 service lists omit newer capabilities. Validate service names/features against current docs.
assistance.analogy: An experienced assistant can propose a diagnosis; measurements and a recovery test establish the outcome.

notes.title: Quota recommendation or application investigation?
notes.flow:
Trusted Advisor check status → EventBridge us-east-1 → SNS
Application telemetry → trace map / older ServiceLens → investigate dependency
paragraphs: Trusted Advisor evaluates supported environment checks across cost, security, resilience, performance, operational excellence and quotas. Service-limit checks flag 80% yellow and 100% red; results are snapshots, not live throughput measurements.

Kinesis shard-count quota is distinct from IncomingBytes/IncomingRecords and throughput-exceeded metrics. Trace correlation needs configured/instrumented telemetry; it does not invent a latency target.

Trusted Advisor events are best effort in us-east-1. Current documentation requires Business Support+, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations for this EventBridge integration; older exam material uses earlier plan names.
notes.trigger: Quota utilisation warning → supported quota check; slow checkout dependency → metrics/logs/traces.
notes.trap: A shard-count quota increase does not itself fix a hot partition key or per-shard throughput throttling.

assistance.flow: Incident → affected scope → connected evidence → reviewed hypothesis → approved repair → verification.

domains.title: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
domains.flow: Signal → correlated evidence → bounded repair → measured outcome

rules.why: Check dimensions, statistic, period and missing data.
Correlate the actual dependency; sampling may hide a trace.
Actor and configuration are different evidence.

rules.choose: Compute, EBS, storage or DB metrics
rules.why: Fix the first saturated dependency; measure before resizing.

domains.notes: Configure collection before expecting evidence. Keep telemetry retention/cost appropriate; use representative windows. Confirm SNS delivery and the resource outcome after automation. Cross-account observability is regional; a multi-Region dashboard does not automatically establish every source link.

domains.title: Reliability and Business Continuity
domains.flow: Healthy capacity → failure isolation → protected history → tested recovery

rules.why: More instances cannot fix a saturated shared database by themselves.
Measure surviving capacity, not only instance count.
A healthy replica may contain the same deletion.
Choose by tested RTO, RPO, cost and dependency readiness.

domains.notes: Availability means usable service now; recovery means rebuilding an acceptable state after failure. Keep caches disposable, durable data protected and failover endpoints/configuration tested. Database restores create new resources: include permissions, networking and endpoint cutover in the recovery clock.

domains.title: Deployment, Provisioning, and Automation
domains.flow: Versioned definition → reviewed change → rollout → health gate → rollback / reconcile

rules.why: Preview does not execute or guarantee success.
Reconcile skipped resources before the next update.
Agent, identity and outbound connectivity are prerequisites.
Deploying copies differs from sharing an existing resource.

domains.notes: Pin the artifact and configuration version. Use a canary/test target before broad changes; limit concurrency, retain rollback inputs and verify application health. Operate existing CI/CD, Git and Terraform workflows; SOA-C03 does not ask you to design a new pipeline.

domains.title: Security and Compliance
domains.flow: Known principal → trusted session → permitted operation → protected data → compliance evidence

rules.why: Trust is not the role’s downstream permission policy.
Key state/context/policy still apply.
An aggregator alone neither records nor repairs.
Patch, restrict or investigate; verify the actual outcome.

domains.notes: Implement the organisation’s supplied controls rather than defining new compliance requirements. Separate identity, permission limits and network reachability. Preserve sensitive investigation evidence; redact secret values from logs and automation output.

domains.title: Networking and Content Delivery
domains.flow: Name → route → filter → listener → target → return path

rules.why: Changing SG rules does not repair a wrong DNS answer.
Check response path and ephemeral ports too.
Endpoint policy limits access; it does not grant IAM permissions.
Lower TTL cannot correct a missing variation dimension.

domains.notes: Trace the actual source and destination; boundaries are not extra appliances. Compare private connectivity, NAT processing, endpoint charges and cross-AZ transfer. Reachability Analyzer tests supported configuration; validate real traffic and application health afterwards.

practice.title: Missing guest metric
practice.prompt: CPU metrics arrive, but an EC2 memory-utilisation alarm has no datapoints. What directly supplies the missing measurement?

choices.text: Enable detailed EC2 monitoring
choices.why: Changes supported built-in metric frequency; it does not collect guest memory.

choices.text: Configure CloudWatch Agent to publish memory usage
choices.why: The agent reads the guest metric and publishes it with configured identity/network access.

choices.text: Create a CloudTrail trail
choices.why: Records AWS API activity, not guest memory usage.

choices.text: Lower the alarm threshold
choices.why: Cannot create missing datapoints.

practice.clue: The metric does not exist yet; frequency and threshold are secondary.
practice.change: If CPU existed but five-minute publication was too coarse, detailed monitoring could be appropriate.
practice.analogy: Install a thermometer before setting its warning temperature.

practice.title: No-data policy
practice.prompt: A continuously reporting heartbeat must alert when publishing stops. With no older real datapoints available, which setting makes missing periods count toward a metric alarm?

choices.text: notBreaching
choices.why: Treats missing values as good for evaluation.

choices.text: ignore
choices.why: Retains the existing state when missing data controls evaluation.

choices.text: breaching
choices.why: Substitutes breaching values when CloudWatch needs missing datapoints.

choices.text: Disable alarm actions
choices.why: Prevents notification, not data loss.

practice.clue: Absence itself is the failure signal. Real evaluation can retrieve older data.
practice.change: For a sparse error-only metric where absence is normal, notBreaching may fit.
practice.analogy: A missed check-in should ring the bell, not count as a healthy check-in.

practice.title: Find the change
practice.prompt: A security group became open just before an incident. Which evidence identifies the API caller and change time?

choices.text: CloudTrail management event
choices.why: Captures supported configuration API activity and caller identity.

choices.text: EC2 CPU graph
choices.why: Shows utilisation, not the actor changing a rule.

choices.text: ALB access log
choices.why: Records requests, not this administrative API operation.

choices.text: AWS Config configuration timeline
choices.why: Shows recorded resource settings and changes, but does not replace CloudTrail API caller evidence.

practice.clue: The question is who changed an AWS setting.
practice.change: If you needed the sequence of recorded rule configurations, Config history would help.
practice.analogy: Consult the change register to find the signatory.

practice.title: Matched but not repaired
practice.prompt: An EventBridge rule matches stopped-instance events, but the Automation never starts. Select TWO first checks.

choices.text: Target invocation permissions and role trust
choices.why: The rule/target needs the appropriate invocation and assumption permissions.

choices.text: FailedInvocations, retry/DLQ and target execution evidence
choices.why: Distinguishes routing success from delivery or execution failure.

choices.text: Only retest the already-matching event pattern
choices.why: Confirms matching again but does not diagnose the failed target invocation.

choices.text: Remove the event pattern to match every event
choices.why: Broadens potentially unsafe actions without fixing target access or delivery.

choices.text: Increase retries without inspecting a permanent AccessDenied
choices.why: Retrying the same permission denial does not repair the policy.

practice.clue: Matching and target invocation are separate boundaries.
practice.change: If the runbook started but failed inside a step, inspect its step output and target resource access.
practice.analogy: A ticket accepted by dispatch may still never reach the technician.

practice.title: Disk bottleneck
practice.prompt: An EC2 service has high EBS latency and queue depth while CPU and memory are healthy. Instance EBS bandwidth has headroom; gp2 burst balance is depleted. What is the most relevant change to evaluate?

choices.text: Enable detailed EC2 monitoring as the performance fix
choices.why: Improves metric frequency but does not add the missing volume I/O capacity.

choices.text: Create a snapshot as the primary latency fix
choices.why: Protects recovery state rather than provisioning sustained volume performance.

choices.text: Move to appropriately provisioned gp3 performance
choices.why: Separates volume performance from capacity; benchmark the required IOPS/throughput.

choices.text: Increase only CPU cores
choices.why: Evidence points to the volume, not CPU.

practice.clue: The exhausted resource is volume I/O, with instance bandwidth ruled out.
practice.change: If the instance EBS bandwidth were saturated, changing only volume IOPS would be insufficient.
practice.analogy: A faster loading dock helps only when the road to it has spare capacity.

practice.title: Database wait evidence
practice.prompt: Writer transaction latency rises with lock waits on a few SQL statements; storage and CPU have headroom. What should you investigate first?

choices.text: SQL, transaction duration and lock contention with Database Insights
choices.why: Directly addresses the measured wait.

choices.text: Double every EC2 web instance
choices.why: Can increase database pressure without fixing locks.

choices.text: Add RDS Proxy without investigating transaction locks
choices.why: Connection pooling does not remove the demonstrated blocking writer transactions.

choices.text: Add a read replica and leave blocking writer transactions unchanged
choices.why: Read scaling does not directly fix the lock contention on the writer.

practice.clue: Wait type identifies a database concurrency issue.
practice.change: If connection setup rather than lock waits dominated, RDS Proxy/connection pooling could be relevant.
practice.analogy: More checkout lanes do not help when one transaction holds the only storeroom key.

practice.title: Shared-file operating boundary
practice.prompt: Two Linux application instances in separate AZs need concurrent access to the same persistent files. Which option directly fits?

choices.text: Regional EFS with mount targets and permitted NFS access
choices.why: Provides supported shared NFS access across AZs; check DNS and mount security.

choices.text: One EBS volume attached across both AZs
choices.why: EBS attachments cannot cross AZ boundaries.

choices.text: Two instance-store directories
choices.why: They are separate local ephemeral storage, not a shared persistent filesystem.

choices.text: Only a CloudFront distribution
choices.why: Caches HTTP content; it is not the requested shared application filesystem.

practice.clue: The required interface is shared files across AZs, not independent block disks.
practice.change: For Windows SMB/AD semantics, consider an appropriate FSx deployment.
practice.analogy: Choose a shared filing room rather than two independent desk drawers.

practice.title: Replica writes: default versus exception
practice.prompt: An RDS MySQL read replica normally rejects writes. An engineer says no write can ever succeed before promotion. Which correction is accurate?

choices.text: read_only=0 can permit writes, but conflicting changes can break replication
choices.why: The default is a control, not an absolute physical impossibility; replica-specific indexes are a documented special case.

choices.text: Any replica write is safe once read_only=0
choices.why: Permitting a write does not protect replication from conflicting application changes.

choices.text: Its endpoint automatically redirects writes to the source
choices.why: The replica has its own endpoint; do not assume transparent write routing.

choices.text: Changing max_allowed_packet makes it a writable primary
choices.why: Message-size limits do not change the replica’s role or consistency model.

practice.clue: Distinguish normally prohibited writes from a documented parameter-controlled exception.
practice.change: If independent application writes are required, use an appropriate writer architecture rather than exploiting a read-replica exception.
practice.analogy: Removing a desk’s read-only sign does not make two clerks’ conflicting ledger edits safe.

practice.title: Replication breaks only on a large message
practice.prompt: MySQL replication works until a large logical message arrives. The source allows a larger max_allowed_packet than the replica. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Matching appropriate source/replica parameter values and the failing message
choices.why: The smaller receiving limit can reject a sufficiently large logical message.

choices.text: The total number of stored database rows
choices.why: Database size does not define this individual-message limit.

choices.text: Only aggregate writes per minute
choices.why: A rate is not the logical size limit that the error identifies.

choices.text: The VPC MTU as if max_allowed_packet were a TCP frame size
choices.why: MySQL logical messages and network frames are different units.

practice.clue: The error identifies message size, not capacity or overall transaction throughput.
practice.change: If the error instead identifies a conflicting local replica write, parameter matching will not repair that inconsistency.
practice.analogy: A letterbox opening limits one envelope, not the total size of the archive.

practice.title: Busy device name after detach
practice.prompt: Evidence identifies a guest driver retaining a device mapping after detach; the EBS volume is otherwise available in the correct AZ. What should be evaluated next?

choices.text: An unused supported attachment name, after checking actual guest mappings
choices.why: The identified collision concerns naming/mapping, not disk I/O performance.

choices.text: More gp2 burst credits
choices.why: Credits affect performance, not resolution of this device-name collision.

choices.text: A cross-AZ attachment to avoid the name
choices.why: EBS attachment must remain in the volume’s AZ.

choices.text: Format the first disk whose name looks similar
choices.why: Names may be remapped; identify the actual volume before touching its data.

practice.clue: The question supplies a specific driver-name cause; do not infer it from every stuck attachment.
practice.change: For a different error such as attachment-count limit, use that control rather than repeatedly renaming devices.
practice.analogy: Two devices cannot claim the same reserved label merely because the storage service calls one available.

practice.title: Resize a public EBS-backed instance
practice.prompt: A compatible EBS-backed On-Demand instance has an auto-assigned public IPv4 and no EIP. Which TWO effects should an operator plan for during an in-place type change?

choices.text: Stop/change/start downtime
choices.why: Changing the type through this workflow requires stopping the instance.

choices.text: The auto-assigned public IPv4 normally changes
choices.why: An Elastic IP would have different address persistence.

choices.text: The instance ID and private IPv4 must always be replaced
choices.why: Those normally persist through ordinary stop/start of the same instance.

choices.text: Instance-store contents are safely retained across the stop
choices.why: Instance-store data is lost; EBS persistence is a different mechanism.

choices.text: ASG membership can never interfere with planned stopping
choices.why: An ASG can mark the stopped instance unhealthy and replace it.

practice.clue: In-place change preserves identity differently from replacement, but needs downtime and address planning.
practice.change: With an EIP, its public address can remain associated; a controlled replacement rollout has a different availability plan.
practice.analogy: The same named machine can reboot on another host while its temporary street number changes.

practice.title: Legacy network-interface bottleneck
practice.prompt: Measurements identify a legacy EC2 virtual network interface as the bottleneck. General application networking is required, not tightly coupled MPI/HPC. Which path should be evaluated?

choices.text: Compatible enhanced networking/ENA and the exact instance’s bandwidth/PPS limits
choices.why: Targets the identified interface capability and measured resource limits.

choices.text: EFA as the universal answer to every packet-rate issue
choices.why: EFA serves specialised tightly coupled communication requirements.

choices.text: Direct Connect as if it replaced the guest instance NIC
choices.why: It supplies hybrid connectivity, not a replacement for this interface capability.

choices.text: A universal 20K-PPS or 25-Gbps ceiling for all modern EC2
choices.why: Legacy exam figures are not per-type modern guarantees.

practice.clue: The workload and measured constraint identify ordinary enhanced networking, not a different network product.
practice.change: For tightly coupled HPC communication, EFA compatibility and application support could become relevant.
practice.analogy: Choose the correct vehicle interface before buying a different intercity road.

practice.title: New launch API versus instance start
practice.prompt: Notify an SNS subscriber when a matching new EC2 launch API operation occurs, including while prior notifications are still being processed. What is the clearest event path?

choices.text: CloudTrail RunInstances event → EventBridge rule → SNS
choices.why: Matches the launch operation; configure the appropriate trail/event and target permissions.

choices.text: Any EC2 running state event, assumed to identify creation uniquely
choices.why: Starting an existing instance can also produce running transitions.

choices.text: One metric alarm held in ALARM for every matching event
choices.why: State-transition notification is not one notification per repeated event.

choices.text: CloudTrail is mandatory for every EventBridge service event
choices.why: EventBridge can also receive direct service events without CloudTrail.

practice.clue: The operation identity is RunInstances; a state name alone is ambiguous.
practice.change: If the requirement is per created instance rather than per API call, extract/process every instance ID from a multi-instance launch event.
practice.analogy: Use the new-order receipt rather than every later “order now active” status change.

practice.title: Test the journey without real users
practice.prompt: Operations needs scheduled browser/API checks with managed metrics and test artifacts even when no customers are active. Which capability most directly fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Synthetics canary
choices.why: Purpose-built scheduled synthetic tests with monitoring integrations and artifacts.

choices.text: ServiceLens / trace map alone
choices.why: Correlates observed telemetry; it does not execute the endpoint test.

choices.text: A dashboard alone
choices.why: Displays existing signals rather than generating test requests.

choices.text: Only a scheduled Lambda invocation, assuming all canary reporting exists automatically
choices.why: Custom Lambda can run checks, but monitoring/reporting/artifacts must be assembled appropriately.

practice.clue: The requirement is active synthetic execution plus managed evidence, not passive correlation.
practice.change: If a bespoke unsupported test executor is required, scheduled custom execution with explicit instrumentation may fit.
practice.analogy: A mystery shopper creates a test visit; a CCTV index only helps inspect visits already recorded.

practice.title: Resize an EBS-root host with scratch data
practice.prompt: A compatible EBS-root EC2 instance also has important temporary results on instance store. It needs more RAM by in-place resizing. What should operations expect?

choices.text: Resize by editing AMI metadata without stopping
choices.why: The running instance’s compute configuration is not changed by editing an image definition.

choices.text: Detach and move instance store to the larger host
choices.why: Instance-store volumes cannot be detached and transferred like EBS volumes.

choices.text: A normal reboot and a stop/start erase the same storage
choices.why: Normal reboot preserves instance-store data; stop/start does not.

choices.text: Copy required scratch data out, then stop/change type/start with downtime
choices.why: EBS-root resizing uses stop/start; EBS data persists, but instance-store data does not.

practice.clue: Root storage is EBS, while additional scratch storage has a different lifecycle.
practice.change: An instance-store-root workload needs migration rather than this normal resize path.
practice.analogy: A persistent filing cabinet and a temporary workbench have different moving rules.

practice.title: Shard quota warning is not a latency trace
practice.prompt: Operations needs supported checks warning about Kinesis shard-count quota utilisation, with a notification on check status changes. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Treat Trusted Advisor results as guaranteed real-time delivery
choices.why: Checks can lag and the EventBridge delivery is best effort; plan eligibility applies.

choices.text: Trusted Advisor → eligible EventBridge integration in us-east-1 → SNS
choices.why: The supported quota check uses environment usage snapshots and check-status events.

choices.text: ServiceLens automatically detects the 80% quota threshold
choices.why: Trace correlation investigates observed application telemetry, not every AWS quota recommendation.

choices.text: Watch only IncomingBytes to determine allocated shard-count quota
choices.why: Data throughput is different from the number of allocated shards against an account quota.

practice.clue: The requirement concerns quota allocation and check status, not one request’s latency.
practice.change: Producer throttling or a hot shard instead requires throughput/error metrics and partition-key investigation.
practice.analogy: A building occupancy inspection is different from timing each service desk.

practice.title: The image has the agent, but telemetry is missing
practice.prompt: A new ASG member boots from an AMI containing the configured CloudWatch Agent. EC2 built-in CPU metrics appear but guest memory metrics do not. What should be checked?

choices.text: Assume ASG reinstalls and starts every agent automatically
choices.why: ASG launches the image; it does not independently guarantee arbitrary guest software startup.

choices.text: Enable detailed monitoring to create the missing memory metric
choices.why: Detailed EC2 monitoring changes built-in frequency, not guest memory collection.

choices.text: Use the original image-source host’s metrics as proof
choices.why: The new member needs its own correctly dimensioned telemetry.

choices.text: Agent startup, configuration, instance-role permission and endpoint connectivity
choices.why: The image supplies software; each running instance must actually start and publish the configured telemetry.

practice.clue: The missing signal is a guest metric, although built-in monitoring works.
practice.change: If only built-in EC2 frequency is required, detailed monitoring can be the relevant choice.
practice.analogy: Packing a measuring tool in the box does not turn it on after delivery.

practice.title: Desired versus actual
practice.prompt: An ASG has actual capacity 3, desired 5 and maximum 10. A ChangeInCapacity policy adds 3. What desired capacity does it request?

choices.why: Adds to actual rather than desired.
The adjustment applies to desired 5; actual is then reconciled toward 8.
The maximum is a cap, not the requested target.
Ignores the scaling adjustment.

practice.clue: Policies change desired capacity, not actual capacity directly.
practice.change: If maximum were 6, the resulting desired capacity would be capped at 6.
practice.analogy: The staffing target changes before the new staff arrive.

practice.title: Cache under write load
practice.prompt: A node-based Redis OSS cluster has one busy primary and several replicas. Write throughput is the bottleneck. What change can distribute key writes when the key distribution supports it?

choices.text: Add replicas only
choices.why: Replicas copy a shard; they do not partition its primary writes.

choices.text: Enable suitable cluster-mode sharding and distribute keys
choices.why: Multiple primaries own different key ranges.

choices.text: Increase CloudFront TTL
choices.why: Does not directly repartition Redis writes.

choices.text: Increase TTL only
choices.why: Changes entry lifetime and potential read misses, not the number of write-owning shards.

practice.clue: Horizontal write scaling needs multiple shards, not more copies of one shard.
practice.change: If reads dominated and stale reads were acceptable, replicas could improve read capacity.
practice.analogy: More photocopies do not create more editors; separate sections can have separate editors.

practice.title: Direct works, ALB fails
practice.prompt: An instance answers on port 8080 directly, but ALB marks it unhealthy. Which investigation is most useful first?

choices.text: Health path/port/matcher and ALB-to-target SG rules
choices.why: The load balancer uses its own configured request and source security boundary.

choices.text: Increase ASG desired capacity before checking the health configuration
choices.why: New instances with the same mismatched health setup can fail identically.

choices.text: Disable all health checks
choices.why: Hides evidence and risks routing to failures.

choices.text: Enable only EC2 status checks in the ASG
choices.why: Does not diagnose or repair the ALB application health-check request.

practice.clue: Direct reachability is not proof that the configured ALB check passes.
practice.change: If every target failed due to a bad application release, roll back the release rather than only changing checks.
practice.analogy: A front entrance working does not prove the inspector’s assigned entrance opens.

practice.title: Standby or reader
practice.prompt: A traditional RDS Multi-AZ DB instance must survive an AZ failure; separate reporting also needs read scaling with acceptable lag. Select TWO appropriate capabilities.

choices.text: Keep Multi-AZ for failover
choices.why: The synchronous standby supports availability.

choices.text: Add a suitable read replica and route reporting reads to it
choices.why: Adds asynchronous read capacity with lag considerations.

choices.text: Read directly from the traditional standby
choices.why: It is not a readable replica endpoint.

choices.text: Keep all reporting on the primary and expect automatic replica routing
choices.why: Applications must use the appropriate read endpoint; creating capacity alone does not redirect queries.

choices.text: Treat a manual snapshot as automatic live database failover
choices.why: Snapshots support recovery; they are not a running synchronous failover target.

practice.clue: Availability and read scaling are separate requirements.
practice.change: A Multi-AZ DB cluster or Aurora has a different readable-instance architecture; inspect the specified deployment model.
practice.analogy: Keep an emergency replacement and a separate reporting desk.

practice.title: Logical deletion
practice.prompt: A valid table was deleted at 10:12; the RDS service is healthy and the standby has the deletion. PITR is enabled and 10:11 is within the recovery window. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Fail over to the standby
choices.why: The logical deletion has already replicated.

choices.text: Restore to a new DB at 10:11, validate and plan cutover
choices.why: Recovers historical state while preserving the source for investigation.

choices.text: Restart the current DB
choices.why: Does not undo committed deletion.

choices.text: Restore only a snapshot taken after the 10:12 deletion
choices.why: A post-deletion recovery point retains the unwanted logical state.

practice.clue: Recover the state before the logical error, not merely a healthy host.
practice.change: For a host failure without logical corruption, managed failover is usually the relevant mechanism.
practice.analogy: A spare ledger with the same erasure cannot recover yesterday’s entry.

practice.title: Prove the recovery objective
practice.prompt: A backup job is green. The runbook promises recovery in one hour with no more than fifteen minutes of lost data. Select TWO necessary validations.

choices.text: Time full restore, dependency setup and application cutover
choices.why: RTO covers usable recovery, not only API acceptance.

choices.text: Check the latest usable recovery point against the incident time
choices.why: Tests whether data loss can meet RPO.

choices.text: Assume green backup means both objectives are met
choices.why: A backup success does not test restoration.

choices.text: Time only the restore API request being accepted
choices.why: Acceptance excludes resource readiness, dependency configuration and usable application cutover.

choices.text: Verify only that a backup plan exists
choices.why: A configured plan does not prove backup job success or a working restore.

practice.clue: Both elapsed outage and recoverable data age need evidence.
practice.change: If only retention compliance were asked, recovery-point retention and vault controls would be central.
practice.analogy: A packed parachute is not the same as a demonstrated safe landing.

practice.title: Version recovery
practice.prompt: An object was overwritten yesterday in an S3 bucket that already had versioning enabled. The previous version is retained. What is the narrowest recovery?

choices.text: Retrieve the retained prior version and verify it before restoring the current object
choices.why: Uses existing object history and avoids broad workload changes.

choices.text: Fail over the RDS database
choices.why: Unrelated to the overwritten S3 object.

choices.text: Enable versioning now and assume it recreates yesterday’s data
choices.why: Cannot retroactively create versions that were not retained.

choices.text: Delete the whole bucket
choices.why: Destroys unrelated data and is unnecessary.

practice.clue: The required historical object version already exists.
practice.change: If versioning was not enabled and no other recovery copy existed, enabling it now could not recover the previous content.
practice.analogy: Use the earlier filing revision rather than replacing the entire office.

practice.title: Deregistered image with retained recovery
practice.prompt: An eligible EBS-backed AMI was accidentally deregistered. A matching Recycle Bin rule already covered it and retention has not expired. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Restore it through the applicable Recycle Bin recovery
choices.why: Preconfigured retention can preserve a deregistered eligible image.

choices.text: Assume every deregistration is immediately unrecoverable
choices.why: That ignores the specified retention mechanism.

choices.text: Create a rule now and expect it to protect past unretained deletions
choices.why: Retention rules are not retroactive recovery of data that was not retained.

choices.text: Assume deregistration already terminated its running instances
choices.why: Deregistration does not itself terminate instances previously launched from the image.

practice.clue: The rule existed before deletion and the retained item is still recoverable.
practice.change: Without applicable retention, investigate surviving snapshots/instances and reconstruct suitable image metadata if possible.
practice.analogy: A pre-arranged recovery bin can hold the discarded plan; adding a bin afterwards cannot recreate an already lost plan.

practice.title: Durable image, unproven application state
practice.prompt: A database application is captured in an EBS-backed AMI. The requirement is application-consistent recovery. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Coordinate application consistency and test recovery; allowing reboot helps flush buffered state
choices.why: Durable captured blocks and a valid boot do not by themselves prove a coherent application transaction state.

choices.text: Selecting No reboot always guarantees application consistency
choices.why: Skipping quiescing/reboot can preserve inconsistent in-memory versus disk state.

choices.text: Provision more IOPS to make an inconsistent image transactionally valid
choices.why: I/O performance cannot reconstruct an uncoordinated application state.

choices.text: Disable No reboot means prevent any reboot
choices.why: It means clearing that option and allowing reboot, not prohibiting it.

practice.clue: Consistency is about a coherent application state, not simply retained bytes.
practice.change: For an already stopped/quiesced application with validated procedures, capture requirements may differ.
practice.analogy: A photograph of durable ledger pages is useful only if the pages describe a consistent point in the transaction.

practice.title: New disk must avoid first-read lazy loading
practice.prompt: A supported restored EBS workload must be fully initialised at volume creation. Which preparation directly addresses that requirement?

choices.text: Enable FSR for the snapshot in the destination AZ, wait ready and check creation credits before creating the volume
choices.why: FSR applies to the relevant snapshot/AZ and eligible new-volume creation.

choices.text: Increase provisioned IOPS alone
choices.why: Configured I/O capacity does not load missing snapshot blocks.

choices.text: Enable FSR only after creating the affected volume
choices.why: It does not retroactively convert that already-created volume into an FSR creation.

choices.text: Enable FSR in an unrelated AZ because snapshots are Regional
choices.why: The FSR preparation is destination-AZ specific despite the snapshot’s Regional scope.

practice.clue: Immediate initialisation and steady-state I/O provisioning are separate mechanisms.
practice.change: If a bounded initialisation interval is acceptable, evaluate current provisioned-initialisation-rate or manual-initialisation options.
practice.analogy: A faster disk motor does not pre-fill the restored pages before the first read.

practice.title: All unhealthy does not mean guaranteed 503
practice.prompt: All registered targets in an ALB target group are unhealthy. Which statement best describes the relevant distinction?

choices.text: ALB can fail open and route to unhealthy targets; actual HTTP results still depend on the request/target
choices.why: Health state is not a universal HTTP status mapping.

choices.text: Every request must receive an ALB-generated 503 solely because health is Unhealthy
choices.why: That confuses all-unhealthy fail-open with conditions such as no registered/all-unused targets.

choices.text: ALB runs a fresh health check before every user request
choices.why: Target health is evaluated periodically.

choices.text: ASG must restart the failed application process instead of replacing an instance
choices.why: ASG instance replacement and application restart are different mechanisms.

practice.clue: Distinguish target health, routing behaviour and the origin of an HTTP status.
practice.change: With healthy B available and cross-zone routing applicable, ALB normally avoids unhealthy A rather than needing all-unhealthy fail-open.
practice.analogy: A dispatcher choosing among bad destinations cannot guarantee what status their doors will return.

practice.title: Repeated cache misses overload an origin
practice.prompt: Several CloudFront cache locations repeatedly fetch the same uncached objects. The goal is to consolidate eligible origin-bound misses with managed CloudFront functionality. What fits?

choices.text: Origin Shield in a supported Region with low latency to the origin
choices.why: Adds a managed caching/consolidation layer before the origin.

choices.text: Weighted DNS alone
choices.why: Distributes DNS answers without inherently consolidating identical origin fetches.

choices.text: Assume Origin Shield is a customer ElastiCache cluster
choices.why: It is part of CloudFront’s managed caching infrastructure.

choices.text: Move the CloudFront distribution into the S3 bucket’s Region
choices.why: A CloudFront distribution is global, not a Regional deployment to relocate.

practice.clue: The missing mechanism is shared origin-miss consolidation, not merely more traffic destinations.
practice.change: If values were custom application session data rather than HTTP object delivery, an application cache could be relevant.
practice.analogy: Several local counters can share one upstream copy desk instead of separately ordering the same item.

practice.title: Protection ends; deletion is separate
practice.prompt: Compliance-mode Object Lock protected a version until yesterday. No legal hold remains and no Lifecycle expiration is configured. Must that version already be gone?

choices.text: No; retention expiry permits eligible deletion but does not schedule it
choices.why: Automatic cleanup needs suitable version-aware Lifecycle rules or another authorised deletion action.

choices.text: Yes, Retain Until Date automatically deletes every version
choices.why: It is a protection deadline, not a deletion job.

choices.text: Lifecycle must delete it even while compliance retention is active
choices.why: Lifecycle cannot override active protection.

choices.text: A delete marker proves every retained version was destroyed
choices.why: A marker and the protected historical versions are distinct objects/states.

practice.clue: Preservation and cleanup are separate controls.
practice.change: If suitable Lifecycle rules were configured, eligible expiration can occur asynchronously after applicable protection ends.
practice.analogy: A contract saying “do not shred before Friday” does not itself order shredding on Friday.

practice.title: Desired fell but four members remain
practice.prompt: An ASG has four healthy in-service members, all protected from scale-in. A valid scale-in changes desired capacity from 4 to 3. What can happen?

choices.text: Desired becomes 3 while actual remains 4 until protection permits removal
choices.why: Desired is a target; protection can prevent convergence without preventing that target update.

choices.text: Desired must remain 4 because protection freezes it
choices.why: Protection controls eligible instance termination, not every desired-capacity change.

choices.text: ASG must terminate an arbitrary protected member immediately
choices.why: The assumed scale-in protection blocks selecting the protected members for ordinary scale-in.

choices.text: All protected members become immune to health replacement
choices.why: Scale-in protection does not prevent unhealthy replacement.

practice.clue: All members are protected from the particular termination path.
practice.change: If a member becomes unhealthy, replacement is a different operation.
practice.analogy: Changing the seat target does not evict a protected occupant.

practice.title: Protected from API termination, then shutdown
practice.prompt: DisableApiTermination is true. An EBS-root ASG member has InstanceInitiatedShutdownBehavior=terminate. Its administrator runs an OS shutdown. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Scale-in protection prevents every unhealthy replacement
choices.why: The health-replacement path is not ordinary scale-in protection.

choices.text: Any AWS service can therefore ignore every protection
choices.why: The documented exceptions do not establish a universal rule for all services or controls.

choices.text: OS shutdown can terminate it; ASG can restore desired capacity
choices.why: API termination protection does not block the specified OS-initiated termination path.

choices.text: EC2 API protection must prevent OS shutdown
choices.why: The OS shutdown behaviour is separate from direct TerminateInstances protection.

practice.clue: The question explicitly supplies the OS terminate setting.
practice.change: With shutdown behaviour stop, it stops first; ASG can subsequently replace the stopped member.
practice.analogy: A lock on the front-door API is not the switch on the machine itself.

practice.title: Restore into AZ B at full initial performance
practice.prompt: A completed Regional snapshot originated from AZ A. New volumes must be created in AZ B with eligible full initial performance. What prepares the restore?

choices.text: Enable FSR for that snapshot in AZ B and wait for readiness plus sufficient credits
choices.why: FSR is configured for the destination snapshot/AZ pair before creating the volume.

choices.text: Enable FSR only in source AZ A
choices.why: The source volume’s location does not initialise a new volume in another destination AZ.

choices.text: Increase IOPS and assume all snapshot blocks are already initialised
choices.why: Provisioned performance and loading snapshot data are separate mechanisms.

choices.text: Enable FSR after creating the affected volume to retroactively initialise it
choices.why: The FSR benefit applies at qualifying new-volume creation, not retroactively to the existing volume.

practice.clue: The deciding location is where the new volume is created.
practice.change: If initialisation delay is acceptable, ordinary restore or supported initialisation-rate options may be more economical.
practice.analogy: Prepare the receiving workshop, not just the workshop the backup came from.

practice.title: Discount commitment does not assure a launch
practice.prompt: A workload must launch matching EC2 capacity in AZ A during an upcoming operation. It already has a Compute Savings Plan. What is still required for capacity assurance?

choices.text: Assume a Regional RI reserves capacity in every AZ
choices.why: Regional RIs provide eligible discounts, not the Zonal capacity reservation.

choices.text: Treat Savings Plan commitment as a maximum charge
choices.why: Unused commitment still costs money; eligible uncovered excess is billed separately.

choices.text: A suitable active AZ Capacity Reservation or matching Zonal RI
choices.why: The billing commitment does not independently hold capacity in the required AZ.

choices.text: Only increase ASG desired capacity
choices.why: Desired is a requested target, not a reservation of available EC2 capacity.

practice.clue: The requirement is availability of matching AZ capacity, beyond pricing.
practice.change: Cost flexibility without a launch-capacity requirement may favour an appropriate Savings Plan alone.
practice.analogy: A discount voucher is not a reserved seat.

practice.title: Offline import followed by archive storage
practice.prompt: An eligible existing Snowball Edge customer imports local data and later archives eligible objects in an S3 Glacier class. What is the correct order?

choices.text: All new customers can order Snowball Edge without restrictions
choices.why: Current availability is limited to existing customers; older exam onboarding assumptions need a caveat.

choices.text: Local copy → return device → AWS imports into S3 → configured Lifecycle transition
choices.why: Physical transfer/import precedes the separate object storage-class transition.

choices.text: Snowball writes straight into Glacier without an S3 import
choices.why: The illustrated import lands in S3; the later Lifecycle action chooses the archive class.

choices.text: A shipped device proves S3 objects are already available
choices.why: Data still must be copied, returned and successfully imported.

practice.clue: The customer is eligible, but import and archive transition are distinct stages.
practice.change: For a new customer, evaluate currently available online or physical-transfer alternatives.
practice.analogy: The courier delivery arrives before the warehouse files it in long-term storage.

practice.title: Failed rollback
practice.prompt: A stack is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED because a required permission was removed. What should the operator do after restoring that permission?

choices.text: Run continue-update-rollback and verify final status
choices.why: Resumes the failed rollback using repaired prerequisites.

choices.text: Create another change set and assume it executes
choices.why: A preview does not resolve a stuck rollback.

choices.text: Delete the production stack immediately
choices.why: Destructive and not required by this failure.

choices.text: Edit only local CDK code without deploying
choices.why: Does not alter the current stack operation.

practice.clue: Rollback itself failed; repair it before another update.
practice.change: For UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE you can plan a corrected new update after inspection.
practice.analogy: Repair the exit route before trying to finish reversing the truck.

practice.title: Drift is not repair
practice.prompt: An operator manually changes a resource setting managed by a CloudFormation stack. What does drift detection do for supported tracked properties?

choices.text: Identifies supported differences against the stack definition
choices.why: Detection reports differences; it is not automatic reconciliation.

choices.text: Repairs every possible property automatically
choices.why: Neither universal coverage nor automatic repair is guaranteed.

choices.text: Treat NOT_CHECKED resources as confirmed IN_SYNC
choices.why: Unsupported or unchecked resources have not been proven free of drift.

choices.text: Rewrites the template to match reality
choices.why: Not an automatic drift-detection effect.

practice.clue: Detection and remediation are separate operations.
practice.change: A deliberately updated template and executed change set could adopt a reviewed intended change.
practice.analogy: An inspection marks the deviation; it does not rebuild the wall.

practice.title: Share versus deploy
practice.prompt: The organisation wants to deploy the same baseline stack in several accounts/Regions, and separately share an existing supported subnet. Select TWO correct tools.

choices.text: StackSets for baseline stack instances
choices.why: Deploys and manages copies with execution controls.

choices.text: RAM for the supported existing subnet share
choices.why: Shares supported resources without recreating them.

choices.text: Use RAM to deploy independent baseline stacks
choices.why: RAM shares supported resources; it is not the stack-copy deployment mechanism.

choices.text: Use an SCP to create the required baseline resources
choices.why: SCPs restrict applicable operations; they do not provision the resources.

choices.text: Assume stack deployment automatically shares every created resource
choices.why: Cross-account sharing requires an appropriate supported sharing configuration.

practice.clue: Deploy copies and share one resource are distinct responsibilities.
practice.change: For one account/Region only, a normal CloudFormation stack may suffice.
practice.analogy: Print copies of the plan with StackSets; grant access to one existing room with RAM.

practice.title: Container rollout failure
practice.prompt: Every new ECS task stops with an image-pull permission error; old tasks remain healthy. What should be examined first?

choices.text: Task execution-role registry permissions and image path/connectivity
choices.why: These govern pulling the image; inspect events for the exact failure.

choices.text: Only the application business-role SQL permissions
choices.why: These apply after startup and do not explain the pull error.

choices.text: Increase task CPU and memory as the permission fix
choices.why: Resources cannot compensate for a denied image-pull operation.

choices.text: Change the application runtime command before fixing the image pull
choices.why: The application command is not reached when its image cannot be pulled.

practice.clue: The failure happens before application execution.
practice.change: If the image pulled but the app failed to query DynamoDB, investigate the task role and app configuration.
practice.analogy: The installer cannot fetch the kit; debugging the installed program is premature.

practice.title: Managed node offline
practice.prompt: A private EC2 instance has SSM Agent installed but appears offline. No inbound SSH is allowed. Select TWO relevant checks.

choices.text: Instance profile and required Systems Manager permissions
choices.why: The agent needs an authorised identity.

choices.text: Outbound HTTPS/DNS access to required service endpoints
choices.why: The agent initiates service connectivity.

choices.text: Open inbound SSH to the world
choices.why: Not required for Systems Manager connectivity.

choices.text: Permit only inbound HTTPS on the instance SG
choices.why: The agent needs outbound service access; opening an inbound port does not supply it.

choices.text: Restart the application process without checking agent identity or network
choices.why: Does not repair the agent prerequisites that determine management connectivity.

practice.clue: Agent, identity and outbound network path are prerequisites.
practice.change: For a running Automation failing an EC2 API step, inspect the automation role rather than only node connectivity.
practice.analogy: A remote technician needs both an access card and a phone line.

practice.title: Bounded operational repair
practice.prompt: A recurring repair needs approval, several AWS API steps, concurrency limits and execution history. What is the best starting capability?

choices.text: Systems Manager Automation runbook
choices.why: Coordinates operational steps with approvals and controls.

choices.text: An untracked SSH command on every instance
choices.why: Lacks the stated coordinated controls.

choices.text: Only an SNS topic
choices.why: Notifies but does not perform the multi-step procedure.

choices.text: A CloudWatch dashboard
choices.why: Visualises evidence without executing the repair.

practice.clue: Repeatable governed maintenance is the requirement.
practice.change: For a simple stateless custom transformation, Lambda may be sufficient; EventBridge can trigger either.
practice.analogy: Use the controlled repair checklist rather than a broadcast message.

practice.title: Repeatable AMI rollout
practice.prompt: A patched AMI has passed tests. New ASG instances must use it, and existing instances must be replaced in controlled batches. Select TWO actions.

choices.text: Publish/select an appropriate launch-template version containing the AMI
choices.why: Defines the artifact used for subsequent launches.

choices.text: Run a configured instance refresh with health/warm-up controls
choices.why: Replaces existing instances gradually under the chosen deployment constraints.

choices.text: Only change a tag on the old instances
choices.why: Does not replace the running machine image.

choices.text: Assume copying an AMI updates running instances
choices.why: AMI creation/copying does not update already running instances.

choices.text: Delete all targets before checking healthy capacity
choices.why: Discards the requested controlled rollout and availability checks.

practice.clue: Artifact selection for new launches and replacement of existing instances are separate steps.
practice.change: If only future scale-out needed the AMI, updating the launch template could be sufficient without refreshing the current fleet.
practice.analogy: Update the installation kit, then schedule controlled replacements.

practice.title: Repair when the agent cannot run
practice.prompt: An important EBS-backed instance has an impaired OS and no working SSM Agent connection. The approved goal is root-volume repair, not replacement. Which capability can fit?

choices.text: A suitable EC2Rescue Automation offline workflow with a temporary helper
choices.why: Automation can orchestrate AWS APIs and offline disk inspection instead of relying on code inside the impaired OS.

choices.text: Repeat Run Command and assume it executes despite the missing agent path
choices.why: Ordinary agent-based commands still need a working managed-node connection.

choices.text: Assume installing the agent in the image proves it is now connected
choices.why: Installed software may be stopped or unable to reach its endpoints.

choices.text: Replace it via ASG while expecting to retain the same repaired OS instance
choices.why: Replacement and repairing this particular root disk are different outcomes.

practice.clue: The target OS is unavailable, but the approved procedure can use external API-driven helper resources.
practice.change: For disposable stateless ASG capacity, replacement may be preferable; do not accidentally mix it with an offline repair procedure.
practice.analogy: Repair the removed disk at a workshop rather than trying to run a command on a machine that cannot boot.

practice.title: Launch from an image is not disk transfer
practice.prompt: An ASG launches another instance from an EBS-backed AMI. The original instance still uses its root volume. What normally happens?

choices.text: Fresh root volumes are created from the AMI’s referenced snapshots
choices.why: The image describes boot metadata and captured disk state; the original working disk remains attached.

choices.text: The original root disk is detached and moved to each new instance
choices.why: That is not the normal image-based launch mechanism.

choices.text: The Launch Template is itself the root disk snapshot
choices.why: It supplies image and launch settings; it is not a disk backup.

choices.text: The snapshot chooses instance type, SG and every launch setting automatically
choices.why: Those launch choices are not all encoded by snapshot data alone.

practice.clue: Image reference and new resource creation differ from reattaching an existing resource.
practice.change: If explicitly recovering one existing data disk, a same-AZ detach/attach workflow is a different operation.
practice.analogy: A photocopied installation image creates another disk; it does not move the original disk.

practice.title: Share for launch versus share for copy
practice.prompt: Another account will launch an instance from a shared unencrypted AMI in the same Region. Must its backing snapshots always be shared separately for that launch?

choices.text: No; AMI sharing provides snapshot access needed for launch
choices.why: Copying the shared image has different backing-storage permission requirements.

choices.text: Yes, launching and copying always have identical permissions
choices.why: This removes the documented distinction between the operations.

choices.text: The AMI must always be copied merely to use another account
choices.why: Same-Region cross-account launch permission can be sufficient in this unencrypted example.

choices.text: The AMI is copied automatically to every AZ
choices.why: An AMI is Regional; another AZ does not require a separate image copy.

practice.clue: Name both the operation and changed boundary: launch, same Region, another account.
practice.change: Encrypted sharing adds eligible KMS access; copying may additionally require storage read permissions.
practice.analogy: Permission to run the installation kit is not identical to permission to copy and redistribute it.

practice.title: An allowed update must not replace the database
practice.prompt: An operator may update a stack. A safeguard must reject accidental replacement of its existing database during updates while preserving ordinary stack administration. Which control fits?

choices.text: Stack termination protection alone
choices.why: Protects deletion of the whole stack, not every replacement during an update.

choices.text: DeletionPolicy: Retain alone
choices.why: Controls resource preservation at deletion/removal boundaries; it is not the requested update-action prohibition.

choices.text: Only grant broader IAM permissions
choices.why: More caller permissions cannot implement a guard against an unwanted protected update.

choices.text: A stack policy denying Update:Replace for that logical resource
choices.why: Stack policies restrict existing-resource update actions independently of the caller’s UpdateStack permission.

practice.clue: The forbidden operation is replacement during a stack update.
practice.change: If the requirement were to prevent deleting the entire stack, choose termination protection.
practice.analogy: Permission to renovate a building is separate from a rule protecting one room.

practice.title: The second Region reports AlreadyExists
practice.prompt: The same account deploys a template in Sydney and Melbourne. Both templates declare RoleName: shared-app. The second fails because the role exists. What is the clearest correction when each deployment needs its own role?

choices.text: Change the instance subnet
choices.why: Subnet placement does not alter the IAM role’s account-wide namespace.

choices.text: Assume no resources were created because the stack failed
choices.why: Earlier successful creates can precede a later failure; inspect rollback and stack events.

choices.text: Generate names or include Region/stack identity
choices.why: IAM names are account-wide although the two owning stacks are Regional.

choices.text: Retry until CloudFormation silently adopts it
choices.why: Matching a name does not automatically import an existing resource into a different stack.

practice.clue: A new create operation is colliding with an account-wide physical name.
practice.change: For one intentionally shared role, keep a single owner and pass its ARN instead of creating it twice.
practice.analogy: Two regional construction teams cannot separately register the same account-wide name.

practice.title: One baseline across account–Region targets
practice.prompt: An operations team must maintain the same approved template in two accounts and two Regions, controlling Region order and rollout concurrency. What fits?

choices.text: Share an AMI instead of deploying the baseline
choices.why: An AMI supplies launch artifacts, not every resource in the infrastructure baseline.

choices.text: CloudFormation StackSets
choices.why: Creates and manages a distinct stack for each selected account–Region combination.

choices.text: One ordinary stack becomes global
choices.why: A normal stack is Regional and does not automatically span target accounts and Regions.

choices.text: Use unrelated templates as an arbitrary dependency graph in one StackSet
choices.why: A StackSet has a common template, not a general workflow for unrelated templates.

practice.clue: The same template is repeated at explicit account–Region targets.
practice.change: Different templates with cross-workflow dependencies need a separate orchestration design.
practice.analogy: One blueprint produces separate buildings; it does not produce one building in four places.

practice.title: Encrypted image moves to another Region
practice.prompt: One account needs to copy its EBS-backed AMI from Sydney to Melbourne. The source snapshots use aws/ebs. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Use the Sydney AMI ID directly in Melbourne
choices.why: AMI IDs and their usable resources are Regional.

choices.text: An ordinary customer-managed key is global
choices.why: KMS keys are Regional; multi-Region keys still have Regional primary/replica resources.

choices.text: A same-account cross-Region copy can use an appropriate destination-Region key
choices.why: The cross-account restriction on sharing aws/ebs does not prohibit this same-account Region-copy workflow.

choices.text: AWS-managed encryption prevents every AMI copy
choices.why: That confuses cross-account key sharing with a separate cross-Region copy operation.

practice.clue: Account ownership stays the same; the Region changes.
practice.change: Another account using the encrypted image also requires appropriate sharing and customer-managed key access.
practice.analogy: Moving a regional copy and lending another company your key are different operations.

practice.title: Snapshots every five minutes
practice.prompt: An existing EBS volume needs a recurring CreateSnapshot request every five minutes. No custom processing is required. Which modern configuration fits?

choices.text: DLM five-minute lifecycle schedule
choices.why: DLM custom snapshot schedules have a one-hour minimum, not the requested five-minute interval.

choices.text: AWS Backup snapshot rule every five minutes
choices.why: Scheduled snapshot-backup rules have a minimum hourly frequency; continuous backup is a different supported-resource feature.

choices.text: Lambda function without a trigger
choices.why: Custom function code does not by itself define recurring execution.

choices.text: EventBridge Scheduler rate(5 minutes) → authorised EC2 CreateSnapshot target
choices.why: Scheduler can invoke the supported API directly; snapshot completion and retention remain separate concerns.

practice.clue: The explicit sub-hour interval changes the otherwise useful managed-lifecycle answer.
practice.change: Hourly EBS creation plus retention/deletion points to DLM; central multi-service protection points to AWS Backup.
practice.analogy: A recurring timer and a retention clerk perform different jobs.

practice.title: Guardrail denial
practice.prompt: A member-account role has an identity Allow for an operation, but an applicable SCP explicitly denies it. What happens?

choices.text: Denied
choices.why: An applicable explicit deny overrides the allow.

choices.text: Allowed because the role is trusted
choices.why: Trust establishes assumption, not exemption from guardrails.

choices.text: Allowed because SCPs grant permissions
choices.why: SCPs limit available permissions; they do not grant an action to a role.

choices.text: Allowed because a permissions-boundary Allow overrides the SCP Deny
choices.why: A boundary is another limit; it cannot override an applicable explicit deny.

practice.clue: An applicable explicit deny is decisive.
