practice.change: If no limiting deny applied, evaluate the remaining applicable permissions and resource-policy conditions.
practice.analogy: A room pass does not override a building-wide prohibition.

practice.title: Continuous property checks
practice.prompt: An operator must record configuration history and continuously evaluate approved resource settings across accounts. Select TWO needed elements.

choices.text: Appropriate Config recorders and rules in source accounts/Regions
choices.why: Produce the history and evaluations.

choices.text: An aggregator for the central supported view
choices.why: Collects views but does not replace source recording.

choices.text: Only an Artifact report
choices.why: Reports AWS compliance evidence, not customer resource changes.

choices.text: Configure only an aggregator and disable source recorders
choices.why: The central view cannot substitute for the required recording/evaluation at sources.

choices.text: Use CloudTrail alone to evaluate and enforce every resource property rule
choices.why: API audit evidence is useful but is not Config configuration-rule evaluation.

practice.clue: Central visibility depends on configured source evidence.
practice.change: To identify which API actor changed a setting, add CloudTrail evidence.
practice.analogy: A central register needs inspections actually performed at each site.

practice.title: Encrypted object denied
practice.prompt: A role can access a bucket, but GetObject fails for an SSE-KMS object using a customer-managed key. Select TWO relevant checks.

choices.text: Key policy/IAM/grants for kms:Decrypt
choices.why: KMS authorisation is distinct from object access.

choices.text: Key state, Region and required encryption context
choices.why: Even otherwise allowed access can fail if the key or context is wrong.

choices.text: Add another s3:GetObject Allow without checking key access
choices.why: Repeating resource permission does not grant the missing cryptographic permission.

choices.text: Assume bucket permission always includes key use
choices.why: Incorrect separation of permissions.

choices.text: Enable key rotation and expect it to override the denied policy
choices.why: Rotation changes cryptographic material management, not authorisation decisions.

practice.clue: The encrypted data and cryptographic key have separate controls.
practice.change: For SSE-S3, customer KMS decrypt permission would not be the corresponding dependency.
practice.analogy: The cabinet pass and the key-use permission are separate.

practice.title: Find the right security source
practice.prompt: A report lists a vulnerable package version on supported EC2 workloads. Which service most directly supplies this assessment?

choices.text: Inspector
choices.why: Assesses supported workload software vulnerabilities/exposure.

choices.text: Macie
choices.why: Discovers sensitive S3 data.

choices.text: GuardDuty
choices.why: Investigates supported threat/activity signals rather than replacing Inspector package assessment.

choices.text: Artifact
choices.why: Provides AWS compliance documentation.

practice.clue: Package vulnerability assessment, rather than data discovery or API auditing.
practice.change: Suspicious credential activity would point toward GuardDuty investigation.
practice.analogy: Use the mechanical inspection report for a faulty component, not a document classification report.

practice.title: Certificate placement
practice.prompt: An ALB in ap-southeast-2 needs an ACM certificate for its HTTPS listener. A matching certificate exists only in us-east-1. What is required?

choices.text: Request/import a suitable certificate in ap-southeast-2 and attach it
choices.why: ALB certificate resources must be in its Region; verify domain validation and hostname coverage.

choices.text: Attach the us-east-1 certificate directly because all ACM certificates are global
choices.why: ACM certificates used by ALB are regional.

choices.text: Change the target group without obtaining a regional listener certificate
choices.why: Backend target selection does not satisfy the frontend certificate Region requirement.

choices.text: Disable TLS permanently
choices.why: Does not meet the HTTPS requirement.

practice.clue: Certificate Region is determined by the TLS termination service.
practice.change: For a CloudFront viewer certificate, ACM in us-east-1 is the required special case.
practice.analogy: The right identity document must be available at the endpoint that presents it.

practice.title: Same-account encrypted ASG launch
practice.prompt: An ASG cannot launch from an image encrypted under a customer-managed key in its own account. The application role has decrypt access. Which identity still needs the documented launch-time key permissions?

choices.text: The ASG service-linked role
choices.why: It participates in provisioning the encrypted volumes before the application instance profile can run.

choices.text: Only the application instance profile again
choices.why: Runtime application permission does not authorise the launch workflow.

choices.text: A new cross-account AssumeRole session, despite same-account ownership
choices.why: No foreign account is specified; assumption is not the missing control in this question.

choices.text: Any IAM user with console sign-in but no key policy access
choices.why: Console authentication does not supply the required KMS authorisation.

practice.clue: The failure precedes application startup; authorise the launch-time service identity.
practice.change: With an external key owner, use the documented cross-account key-policy and grant workflow.
practice.analogy: Give the installation crew permission to open the kit; the eventual resident’s key is a different permission.

practice.title: Cross-account key: grant, not role assumption
practice.prompt: The ASG is in account A; its image’s snapshots use a customer-managed KMS key in account B. AMI access is valid. Which additional AWS-documented combination enables the ASG launch identity?

choices.text: Suitable key policy plus an explicit KMS grant to the ASG service-linked role
choices.why: The external key owner must authorise the documented cross-account grant path.

choices.text: Only AssumeRole into account B with no key grant
choices.why: Role assumption is not the prescribed ASG service-linked-role KMS grant mechanism.

choices.text: Only add the app instance profile to an S3 bucket policy
choices.why: That addresses neither the launch-time identity nor the encrypted EBS key.

choices.text: Copy and re-encrypt as the only possible solution
choices.why: That can be an alternative, but is not mandatory when supported key-policy/grant access is configured.

practice.clue: The deciding fact is that key ownership differs from ASG ownership.
practice.change: For a same-account key, configure the service-linked role’s documented key policy instead of assuming foreign ownership.
practice.analogy: The other building can authorise a specific installation crew through a key grant without lending that crew an employee identity.

practice.title: Object access audit coverage and cost
practice.prompt: A management-event trail exists. The team needs CloudTrail identity evidence for S3 GetObject operations. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Configure appropriate object data-event selectors and account for data-event charges
choices.why: Management events alone do not provide the requested object-level coverage.

choices.text: Assume management event history already includes every GetObject
choices.why: Object data operations require their own applicable logging configuration.

choices.text: Treat best-effort server access logs as a guaranteed immediate complete CloudTrail feed
choices.why: Different delivery/completeness and identity-evidence semantics apply.

choices.text: Assume no S3 server-log delivery fee means every logging destination and query is free
choices.why: Storage/access/analysis cost remains, and other delivery destinations can have ingestion charges.

practice.clue: Choose the evidence type and event coverage before assuming a trail satisfies the audit requirement.
practice.change: For best-effort access analysis with logs delivered to S3, the service’s direct delivery fee model differs.
practice.analogy: A register of administrative changes does not automatically contain every document read.

practice.title: Copy HR and Audit objects into Finance
practice.prompt: A Finance identity can write its destination bucket. HR and Audit must permit that identity to copy selected source objects. Which approach keeps the permission path simplest?

choices.text: Grant only source GetObject because CopyObject needs no destination permission
choices.why: The operation also requires the applicable destination PutObject permission.

choices.text: Grant Finance source GetObject in its identity policy and source bucket policies, keeping Finance credentials
choices.why: The same copy credentials can then satisfy both source reads and destination writes.

choices.text: Assume an HR role and automatically inherit Finance write access
choices.why: Assumed-role credentials do not union their permissions with the original user’s Finance permissions.

choices.text: Put a role trust policy on the S3 bucket
choices.why: S3 bucket policies grant resource access; an IAM role trust policy governs role assumption.

practice.clue: The same effective principal must be allowed at both ends.
practice.change: A deliberately authorised source role could work if it also has the destination access; it is not automatic.
practice.analogy: Changing badges does not keep the doors your previous badge opened.

practice.title: Private S3 route
practice.prompt: Private EC2 instances in one VPC need same-Region S3 API access without NAT. What is usually the appropriate lowest-overhead endpoint?

choices.text: S3 gateway endpoint associated with relevant route tables
choices.why: Provides a prefix-list route; IAM/bucket/KMS access still applies.

choices.text: Internet gateway alone with no addressing changes
choices.why: Does not give private-only IPv4 instances direct internet access.

choices.text: A DNS alias without any network path
choices.why: Names do not provide routing.

choices.text: An S3 gateway endpoint security group
choices.why: Gateway endpoints do not use interface ENI security groups.

practice.clue: Same-VPC gateway endpoint use case, not remote on-premises access.
practice.change: For supported remote/hybrid S3 access through private ENIs, consider an interface endpoint and its DNS/cost model.
practice.analogy: Choose the direct service road instead of buying an internet exit.

practice.title: Private egress cost
practice.prompt: A zonal NAT gateway in AZ A carries large egress from workloads in AZ B. Which change should be evaluated against availability and cost requirements?

choices.text: AZ-aligned NAT paths and applicable service endpoints
choices.why: Can reduce cross-AZ dependency/transfer; compare added NAT hourly cost and endpoint charges.

choices.text: Assume every additional NAT is always cheaper
choices.why: Hourly and volume costs vary.

choices.text: Send arbitrary internet egress through an S3 gateway endpoint
choices.why: The endpoint routes supported S3 traffic; it is not a general internet egress service.

choices.text: Choose interface endpoints for every service without comparing charges
choices.why: Availability, service support, hourly cost, data processing and AZ traffic still need evaluation.

practice.clue: Compare processing, cross-AZ transfer and availability together.
practice.change: At very low volume a central path may be cheaper if its resilience trade-off is accepted.
practice.analogy: A local exit avoids a cross-town trip, but another exit has its own upkeep cost.

practice.title: Private-name resolution
practice.prompt: An AWS instance resolves an internal private hosted-zone name, but on-premises clients cannot. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Resolver inbound endpoint, conditional forwarding and its network path
choices.why: Enables hybrid clients to query the appropriate AWS resolver path.

choices.text: Change only a public hosted-zone record for the private name
choices.why: Does not configure on-premises access to the intended private DNS view.

choices.text: Add only an AWS outbound Resolver endpoint for queries coming from on premises
choices.why: Inbound and outbound endpoint directions differ; remote queries need the appropriate inbound resolution path.

choices.text: Lower the private record TTL without establishing forwarding
choices.why: Changes cache time, not access to the resolver that can answer the private name.

practice.clue: The failure is scoped to hybrid DNS clients.
practice.change: If DNS answered correctly but the TCP connection timed out, investigate routes/filters/target.
practice.analogy: The address exists in the branch directory but the head office cannot reach that directory.

practice.title: Incorrect cached language
practice.prompt: CloudFront forwards lang to an origin that varies content by language, but its cache key ignores lang. Users receive another language. What fixes correctness?

choices.text: Include lang in the appropriate cache policy and address existing entries
choices.why: Separates response variants.

choices.text: Lower TTL only
choices.why: Shortens the wrong sharing interval without fixing the key.

choices.text: Add lang only to the origin request policy, leaving the cache key unchanged
choices.why: Forwarding a value does not necessarily partition cached responses by that value.

choices.text: Add an unrelated header to the cache key while still ignoring lang
choices.why: Does not distinguish the response dimension causing the incorrect language reuse.

practice.clue: The cache treats different content variants as the same key.
practice.change: If the response never varied by language, excluding lang would improve reuse without harming correctness.
practice.analogy: Different editions need different shelf labels.

practice.title: Response-only block
practice.prompt: For a browser connection browser:54321 → ALB:443, a stateless subnet NACL permits inbound 443 but blocks outbound destination 54321. What occurs?

choices.text: The response can be blocked; allow the relevant ephemeral return range
choices.why: NACLs independently evaluate both directions.

choices.text: The inbound rule automatically permits the return
choices.why: That describes stateful SG handling, not NACLs.

choices.text: Change only the backend SG to repair the ALB subnet outbound NACL
choices.why: A different security boundary cannot override this explicit return-path filter.

choices.text: Outbound destination 443 alone fixes this browser response
choices.why: The browser response destination is its ephemeral port.

practice.clue: Response destination differs from request destination.
practice.change: For a security group tracking the established allowed flow, return traffic is automatically permitted.
practice.analogy: A two-way trip needs the return gate open too.

practice.title: Model versus live traffic
practice.prompt: Reachability Analyzer reports a supported path reachable, but the application still times out. Select TWO useful next checks.

choices.text: Application listener, target health and OS firewall
choices.why: Configuration modelling does not prove the process is accepting traffic.

choices.text: Actual flow/access logs and measured network/application outcome
choices.why: Tests real requests at the relevant time and source.

choices.text: Conclude every packet must succeed
choices.why: Modelled reachability is not a live traffic guarantee.

choices.text: Assume a correct DNS answer proves the application is healthy
choices.why: Name resolution does not prove the target process is listening or responding.

choices.text: Treat Flow Logs ACCEPT as business success
choices.why: Acceptance is not an application result.

practice.clue: A configuration model and a live application test prove different things.
practice.change: If the model identified a blocking route, correct that proven dependency before application tuning.
practice.analogy: A clear road map does not prove the shop is open.

practice.title: Same VPC, different subnet, SQL timeout
practice.prompt: An EC2 app and RDS MySQL instance use different subnets in one VPC. Local routes are intact, NACLs permit both directions, DNS is correct and MySQL is listening. The DB SG has no app ingress. What fixes the first proven block?

choices.text: Allow the database port from the app SG in the DB SG
choices.why: The routing path exists; resource-level ingress is missing.

choices.text: Create VPC peering between the two subnets
choices.why: Peering joins VPCs, not subnets already sharing the VPC local path.

choices.text: Add a NAT gateway to the database subnet
choices.why: NAT is not required for this same-VPC private database connection.

choices.text: Grant the app role AdministratorAccess
choices.why: IAM permissions do not open the database’s network security group.

practice.clue: Evidence already establishes routing; the missing control is database ingress.
practice.change: If the route were blackholed by a deliberate routing change, fix the proven path first.
practice.analogy: The road reaches the building, but its gate still needs to admit the visitor.

practice.title: Custom NACL starts closed
practice.prompt: A routed app-to-DB path uses a newly created custom NACL with no allow rules and a new DB SG with no inbound rules. Which TWO configurations are needed for the assumed TCP path?

choices.text: DB SG ingress on the database port from the app SG
choices.why: New custom SGs do not start with arbitrary inbound access.

choices.text: Custom NACL rules for the request and relevant return traffic
choices.why: A custom NACL initially denies and is stateless.

choices.text: Rely on the default NACL allow rules in this custom NACL
choices.why: A newly created custom NACL does not inherit the default NACL’s allow-all rules.

choices.text: Assume the default SG self-reference opens every new SG
choices.why: That self-reference applies to the default SG’s members, not every group.

choices.text: Enable an egress-only IGW for private IPv4 SQL
choices.why: An egress-only IGW is IPv6 internet egress, not this local SQL path.

practice.clue: Name the exact initial control type: custom NACL and custom SG.
practice.change: With an unchanged default NACL, its initial allow rules would remove that particular NACL block; DB SG ingress could still be needed.
practice.analogy: A new checkpoint can start shut even though the site’s original checkpoint started open.

practice.title: Public route but no public IPv4
practice.prompt: A subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to an IGW, but an instance has only private IPv4. Filters are valid. What is still needed for direct IPv4 internet access?

choices.text: Suitable public IPv4/EIP addressing on the instance
choices.why: The IGW route alone does not supply a direct public IPv4 identity.

choices.text: Only a larger instance type
choices.why: CPU and memory do not supply missing public addressing.

choices.text: An egress-only IGW for its private IPv4
choices.why: That gateway supports IPv6, not direct IPv4 connectivity.

choices.text: A different subnet name
choices.why: Names do not change addressing, routes or traffic controls.

practice.clue: Direct IPv4 access requires both the path and suitable public addressing.
practice.change: If the instance must remain private, use an appropriate NAT/endpoint path instead of direct public addressing.
practice.analogy: An exit road does not automatically give the vehicle a public return address.

practice.title: IPv6 outbound only
practice.prompt: Instances with deliberately assigned IPv6 addresses need outbound internet connections and replies, with no new inbound internet connections. Which gateway fits?

choices.text: Egress-only internet gateway with the IPv6 route and controls
choices.why: Designed for outbound-initiated IPv6 internet communication.

choices.text: Public NAT gateway as if it were an IPv6 egress-only IGW
choices.why: Private IPv4 NAT egress and native IPv6 outbound-only routing are different mechanisms.

choices.text: Only an IPv4 route to an IGW
choices.why: An IPv4 route does not route the separate IPv6 address space.

choices.text: No configuration because every EC2 instance automatically has IPv6
choices.why: IPv6 CIDR/address assignment and routing are not automatic for every instance.

practice.clue: The protocol and initiation direction jointly decide the gateway.
practice.change: For private IPv4 outbound internet traffic, a suitable NAT path would be relevant.
practice.analogy: Choose the gate for the address family printed on the vehicle’s address.

practice.title: Private origin and website endpoint
practice.prompt: A distribution uses an S3 website endpoint. The requirement is authenticated CloudFront-only S3 access using OAC. Which change fits?

choices.text: Use the S3 REST origin with appropriate OAC and a scoped bucket policy
choices.why: OAC supports the REST-origin model; the website endpoint remains a custom HTTP origin.

choices.text: Attach OAC directly to the website endpoint
choices.why: OAC/OAI do not apply to the website custom-origin endpoint.

choices.text: Add HTTPS to the S3 website endpoint URL and assume support
choices.why: S3 website endpoints do not provide HTTPS themselves.

choices.text: Treat a secret Referer header as equivalent to OAC authentication
choices.why: A spoofable header condition is a limited workaround, not the same trust mechanism.

practice.clue: The origin endpoint type determines the authentication and transport features available.
practice.change: When website behaviour is deliberately retained, evaluate its custom-origin limitations rather than claiming OAC support.
practice.analogy: A different sign above the website entrance does not turn it into the authenticated API entrance.

practice.title: Explicit S3 wrong-signing-Region error
practice.prompt: A bucket name was deleted and recreated in Singapore. CloudFront receives AuthorizationHeaderMalformed: signed for ap-southeast-2, expected ap-southeast-1. What should be corrected first?

choices.text: Refresh/update the origin’s current bucket information, deploy and verify the signing scope
choices.why: The explicit response identifies stale origin/signing Region information.

choices.text: Assign a home Region to the access key
choices.why: Access keys do not carry that Regional ownership property.

choices.text: Move the global CloudFront distribution to Singapore
choices.why: A distribution is not a Regional resource to move.

choices.text: Only open a VPC SG because every authorisation error is a timeout
choices.why: S3 returned an explicit HTTP error; that is not evidence of a failed network connection.

practice.clue: Resource location and signature scope must agree; neither is a JSON-body routing field.
practice.change: A timeout without an S3 response would require a different connectivity investigation.
practice.analogy: The parcel arrived, but the signed identity scope named the wrong regional authority.

practice.title: Public destination does not select peering
practice.prompt: Two EC2 workloads in ordinary AWS Regions use public IP addresses. A peering connection is then created, but requests still target those public IPs. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: AWS documents AWS-to-AWS public-IP traffic staying on its network, and peering needs private destinations/routes
choices.why: Public addressing is separate from the physical AWS network path; peering does not rewrite those requests.

choices.text: Public addressing always proves external-internet transit
choices.why: Current AWS guidance contradicts that blanket statement; China/Sovereign Cloud exceptions are separately documented.

choices.text: Peering automatically redirects every public-IP call
choices.why: Peering routes private connectivity; merely creating it does not change public-IP destinations.

choices.text: Direct Connect is automatically inserted
choices.why: Direct Connect is a separately provisioned network connection, not an automatic EC2 communication hop.

practice.clue: Address selection and connectivity configuration have not changed.
practice.change: A private-address requirement needs suitable private routes/connectivity and permitted traffic.
practice.analogy: A public street address does not identify which owned road carried the delivery.

theory.title: Provision / configure
theory.purpose: Review the intended resource configuration and artifact before an operational change.
theory.dependencies: Versioned template, image, role, quota and free subnet IPs.
theory.failure: A deployment fails or creates drift from intended state.
theory.evidence: Stack events, change set, image/task status and CloudTrail actor.
theory.verify: Fix the prerequisite, complete rollback/reconcile and verify deployed state.

theory.title: Operate
theory.purpose: Keep the workload serving within its availability, latency and cost constraints.
theory.dependencies: Healthy targets, runtime identity, database, storage and network.
theory.failure: Instance running but unhealthy, or insufficient surviving capacity.
theory.evidence: Target health, scaling activities, guest metrics and DB load.
theory.verify: Restore usable capacity and verify the same user path under representative load.

theory.title: Observe
theory.purpose: Collect the metrics, logs, traces and relevant resource/API events needed to distinguish failures.
theory.dependencies: Agent/instrumentation, permissions, dimensions, retention and cross-account links.
theory.failure: An alarm has no data or the useful log/trace was never collected.
theory.evidence: Publication timestamps, alarm history, log streams and collection errors.
theory.verify: Repair collection, send a known test event and verify both evidence and alert delivery.

theory.title: Investigate
theory.purpose: Trace symptom → affected scope → evidence → likely cause. Identify the first boundary with a proven fault.
theory.dependencies: Correct account, Region, AZ, time window, principal and request correlation.
theory.failure: Treating a correlation or assistant recommendation as a confirmed cause.
theory.evidence: Logs/trace timing, API changes, configuration history and service health.
theory.verify: Choose a test that distinguishes the likely cause from the nearest alternative.

theory.title: Remediate
theory.purpose: Perform the smallest approved corrective action, with safe targeting, retries and rollback.
theory.dependencies: Scoped role, runbook, preconditions, approvals and concurrency/error limits.
theory.failure: A broad repair damages healthy resources or loops on its own events.
theory.evidence: Runbook step output, target API error and resulting resource state.
theory.verify: Confirm the exact action and retry safely; remove the cause, not just the symptom.

theory.title: Validate / recover
theory.purpose: Prove service and data recovery against actual RTO/RPO, then prevent recurrence.
theory.dependencies: Usable recovery point, KMS access, target network, dependency order and cutover plan.
theory.failure: Backup succeeds but restore, access or application cutover fails.
theory.evidence: Restore job, record checks, endpoint tests, elapsed outage and data age.
theory.verify: Verify business results and recovery objectives; record prevention in controlled configuration.

theory.title: User request
theory.purpose: Resolve a name, connect to the advertised endpoint and send the application request.
theory.dependencies: DNS response, client network, TLS trust and caller identity as required.
theory.failure: The name is wrong or a certificate does not match.
theory.evidence: DNS answers, served certificate and client-visible status/timing.
theory.verify: Retest from the affected source and account for DNS caches.

theory.title: Route / filter
theory.purpose: Apply cache/origin behaviour and listener routing to an eligible backend.
theory.dependencies: Routes, SG/NACL, return path, health check and target port.
theory.failure: A good DNS answer reaches a blocked or unhealthy target.
theory.verify: Correct the first failed hop and verify request plus response.

theory.title: Application
theory.purpose: Use the deployed artifact and runtime identity to process the request and construct a response.
theory.dependencies: CPU, memory, dependencies, role permissions, configuration and state.
theory.failure: A bad rollout, exhausted resource or denied downstream request.
theory.evidence: Version, logs, traces, utilisation, failed API action and status checks.
theory.verify: Rollback or repair the measured dependency; verify latency, errors and business outcome.

theory.title: Durable state
theory.purpose: Preserve the authoritative data and independent recoverable history.
theory.dependencies: Storage performance, database consistency, backups, encryption and access.
theory.failure: Slow I/O, logical corruption, inaccessible key or unusable recovery point.
theory.evidence: DB waits, volume metrics, version/recovery timestamp and KMS errors.
theory.verify: Restore/tune the right layer and validate integrity before cutover.
